topics.title: Uniform circular motion: angular speed, period and frequency

learn.hook: A ceiling fan, a Ferris wheel at a Dussehra mela and the Earth's spin all share one set of simple formulas.
points: Uniform circular motion (UCM): constant speed on a circle. Speed is constant but velocity keeps changing direction.
Angular displacement Δθ (in radians); angular speed ω = dθ/dt (rad s⁻¹). Linear speed v = Rω.
Period T is the time for one revolution; frequency ν = 1/T (Hz or rev s⁻¹). ω = 2π/T = 2πν, v = 2πRν.
Centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/R = ω²R = 4π²ν²R.

example.q: A stone tied to a 0.5 m string is whirled at ω = 4 rad s⁻¹. Find its speed and centripetal acceleration.

learn.reallife: A washing machine's drum spinning at 1200 rpm (20 rev s⁻¹) has ω = 40π rad s⁻¹, enough to fling water out of clothes.

quiz.q: A particle moves on a circle of radius 3 m with angular speed 2 rad s⁻¹. Its linear speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: v = Rω = 3 × 2 = 6 m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: A wheel makes 10 revolutions in 5 s. Its frequency in Hz is
quiz.explain: ν = revolutions/time = 10/5 = 2 Hz.

quiz.q: A body moves on a circle of radius 2 m at 4 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: a_c = v²/R = 16/2 = 8 m s⁻².

quiz.explain: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π rad s⁻¹.

quiz.explain: Only the magnitude of velocity (speed) is constant; directions keep changing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks velocity is constant when speed is

A is true but R is false

teach.ask: Gappu spins on a merry-go-round and is puzzled: 'My speed is constant, so where is the acceleration?' Explain angular speed, period, frequency and v = Rω.

teach.nudge: If speed is constant, what about velocity changes? How are ω, T and ν connected?

topics.title: Centripetal acceleration: derivation and nature

learn.hook: A centrifuge at an AIIMS blood bank can produce accelerations over 1000 times g, all pointing towards the centre.
points: Derivation: in time Δt the velocity turns through Δθ; the triangle of velocity vectors is similar to the triangle of position vectors, so |Δv|/v = |Δr|/R.
Dividing by Δt and letting Δt → 0: a = v·(v/R) = v²/R, directed towards the centre (Δv points inward in the limit).
Magnitude v²/R is constant, but the direction keeps changing (always towards the centre), so the centripetal acceleration is NOT a constant vector.
Only in uniform circular motion is the net acceleration purely radial; if speed changes, there is also a tangential component.

topics.title: Force, Aristotle's fallacy and Galileo's inclines

learn.hook: Stop pedalling your cycle and it slows down. For 2000 years people concluded that motion needs a constant push. They were wrong.
points: Kinematics describes motion; dynamics asks what causes motion and changes in motion. The answer is force.
A force is needed to change a body's velocity (speed or direction), not to keep it moving. Forces may act by contact (push, friction, tension) or at a distance (gravity, magnetic, electric).
Aristotle's fallacy: an external force is needed to keep a body moving uniformly. Wrong, because he missed friction and air resistance, which oppose motion; the push only cancels them.
Galileo's inclined planes: a ball speeds up rolling down, slows down rolling up, and on a horizontal plane its speed should stay constant if there is no friction.

example.q: A cart is pushed along a road at constant speed with a 50 N force. Why does it need the push at all, and what does that say about Aristotle's idea?
steps: At constant velocity, the net force on the cart is zero.
So the 50 N push must be balanced by 50 N of friction and air resistance.
The push cancels opposing forces; it is not needed for motion itself. Aristotle's view overlooked friction.
example.answer: The push only balances friction; net force is zero

learn.reallife: A hockey puck on smooth ice at an indoor rink in Gurugram glides far without any push because friction is tiny.

teach.praise: Friction was the sneaky villain! Without it, my car would roll on forever.
teach.nudge: What force did Aristotle forget? And what is force really needed for?

topics.title: Inertia and Newton's first law

learn.hook: Pull a tablecloth fast enough and the dishes stay put. That stubbornness of matter has a name: inertia.
points: Galileo's double incline: a ball rolling down one incline climbs the other to nearly the same height. Make the second incline gentler and it travels farther; make it horizontal and, without friction, it would roll forever.
So rest and uniform straight-line motion are equivalent states: in both, no net force acts.
Inertia is the resistance of a body to any change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Mass is the measure of inertia.

Ancient Indian thought: the Vaisheshika idea of 'vega' (a tendency to keep moving in a straight line) came close to inertia, and Bhaskara II's (1150 CE) 'tatkaliki gati' anticipated instantaneous motion.
Newton's first law: every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by an external net force to change that state.

example.q: In Galileo's double incline, the first plane is released from 20 cm height. The second plane is made less steep. What happens?
steps: Without friction, the ball rises to the same 20 cm height.
A gentler slope means a longer path to reach 20 cm.
With the slope reduced to zero, it never reaches 20 cm, so it rolls on forever.
example.answer: It travels farther; on a level plane it would never stop

learn.reallife: When a spent stage of an ISRO rocket separates in space, it keeps coasting at the velocity it had: inertia at work.

teach.ask: Gappu asks why passengers' heads jerk and why a tablecloth trick works. Explain inertia and state Newton's first law.
teach.praise: Matter is lazy about changing what it's doing: that's inertia. And only a net force can change it!
teach.nudge: What property keeps things doing what they were doing? What does it take to change that?

topics.title: First law in action, and momentum

learn.hook: A cricket ball and a tennis ball at the same speed: one you can catch bare-handed, the other stings. The difference is momentum.
points: First law, equivalent form: if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero (and vice versa).
A book on a table: weight down is balanced by the normal force up, so a = 0. A spaceship far from all stars needs no engine to keep moving uniformly.
Passengers lurch backward when a bus starts suddenly and forward when it brakes: their bodies tend to keep their earlier state.
An astronaut who leaves an accelerating spaceship has zero acceleration the moment he is outside (no force from the ship, gravity negligible in deep space).
Momentum p = mv is a vector along v. Catching a fast ball, stopping a bullet, or a karate chop all show that the effect of a blow depends on momentum and on how fast it changes.

example.q: A spaceship in deep space accelerates at 100 m s⁻². An astronaut drifts out of the hatch. What is his acceleration just after leaving?
steps: Inside, the ship's floor pushes him, giving 100 m s⁻².
Outside, nothing pushes him and gravity from distant stars is negligible.
Net force = 0, so his acceleration is 0 (he keeps the velocity he had).

learn.reallife: In a crowded DTC bus, standing passengers grab the handle when it suddenly brakes, because their bodies keep moving forward by inertia.

teach.nudge: Did a force push you forward, or did your body just keep doing something? What is momentum?

topics.title: Newton's second law: F = dp/dt and F = ma

learn.hook: Push a shopping trolley at a supermarket: empty, it zips; loaded, it crawls. Same push, different acceleration.
points: Second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net applied force and takes place in the direction of the force: F = dp/dt.
For constant mass, F = m dv/dt = ma. 1 newton = force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
F = 0 gives a = 0, so the second law agrees with the first.
Component form: Fₓ = maₓ, F_y = ma_y, F_z = ma_z. A force changes only the velocity component along it (a force ⊥ v changes direction, not speed).
The law is local: the acceleration at an instant depends on the net force at that same instant, not on past forces.

example.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg block. Find the acceleration and the velocity after 3 s, starting from rest.

learn.reallife: When a cricket ball leaves the bowler's hand, its acceleration depends only on the forces at that instant (gravity and air), not on the bowler's push a moment ago.

topics.title: Second law in action: bullets, impulse and batsmen

learn.hook: A batsman meets a 140 km/h bouncer for a few milliseconds. In that blink, the force on the bat can reach thousands of newtons.
points: The second law applies to a particle, and also to a rigid body or a whole system, using the net EXTERNAL force and the acceleration of the system.
Impulse = F × Δt = change in momentum Δp. Impulsive forces are large and act for a very short time (bat on ball, hammer on nail); we measure their effect by Δp.
Bullet stopped in a block: find a from v² = u² + 2as, then F = ma.
If y = ut + ½gt² describes a particle (x-motion uniform), then a = g along y, so F = mg along y: a constant force gives a parabolic path.
Ball hit straight back at the same speed: Δp = m(v − (−v)) = 2mv.

example.q: A 0.15 kg cricket ball moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is hit straight back at 20 m s⁻¹. Find the impulse and the average force if contact lasts 0.01 s.
steps: Take the ball's return direction as +: initial p = −0.15 × 20 = −3 kg m s⁻¹, final p = +3 kg m s⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Fielders pull their hands back while catching to increase the contact time, reducing the force for the same change in momentum.

topics.title: Newton's third law

learn.hook: When you push a wall, the wall pushes you back just as hard. Then why don't the two pushes cancel? This is the most misunderstood law in physics.
points: Third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. F_AB = −F_BA (force on A by B equals minus force on B by A).
Action and reaction act at the same instant on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel each other.
There is no cause and effect between them: either force can be called the action.
In a system of bodies, internal forces come in third-law pairs and cancel; so only external forces affect the motion of the whole system.
Two colliding billiard balls exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so they receive equal and opposite impulses.

example.q: A 50 kg girl on skates pushes a 25 kg boy on skates with 100 N. Find each one's acceleration.
steps: The boy gets 100 N forward: a = 100/25 = 4 m s⁻².
By the third law, the girl gets 100 N backward: a = 100/50 = 2 m s⁻² backward.
Equal forces, unequal accelerations, because masses differ.
example.answer: Boy 4 m s⁻², girl 2 m s⁻² opposite

learn.reallife: When an Indian Navy sailor fires a deck gun, the gun recoils: the shell pushes back on the gun with the same force the gun pushes the shell.

games.title: Action–reaction
items: Action and reaction act on the same body.
They act on different bodies.
Action and reaction are equal in magnitude at every instant.
F_AB = −F_BA always.
The reaction comes slightly after the action.
They are simultaneous.
A horse pulling a cart and the cart pulling the horse are an action–reaction pair.
They act between the same two bodies.
Weight of a book and normal force of the table on it form an action–reaction pair.
Both act on the book; the pair of weight is the book's pull on the Earth.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'If action and reaction are equal and opposite, they cancel, so nothing can ever move!' Explain where his reasoning breaks.
teach.praise: They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they can't cancel each other. Phew, I can still fly!
teach.nudge: Do action and reaction act on the same body or on different bodies?

topics.title: Rockets, recoil and conservation of momentum

learn.hook: Chandrayaan-3's rocket had nothing to 'push against' in space. It moved by throwing gas backward: momentum must be conserved.
points: Third-law examples: walking (foot pushes ground back, ground pushes you forward), rowing (oar pushes water back), rocket (rocket pushes gas backward, gas pushes rocket forward), gun recoil.
Law of conservation of momentum: the total momentum of an isolated system (no net external force) stays constant.
Derivation for a collision: F_AB Δt = Δp_A and F_BA Δt = Δp_B; since F_AB = −F_BA, Δp_A + Δp_B = 0.
Recoil of a gun (initially at rest): 0 = m_b v_b + M V → V = −m_b v_b/M.
A shell exploding in flight: internal forces cannot change the total momentum; the fragments' momenta add up to the shell's momentum just before the explosion.

example.q: A 4 kg gun fires a 0.02 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
steps: V = −8/4 = −2 m s⁻¹ (opposite to the bullet).

learn.reallife: ISRO's PSLV and GSLV rockets throw out exhaust gases at kilometres per second; the forward momentum of the rocket equals the backward momentum of the gas.

games.title: Deriving conservation of momentum in a collision
items: Force on A by B acts for time Δt: F_AB Δt = Δp_A
Force on B by A acts for the same Δt: F_BA Δt = Δp_B
Third law: F_AB = −F_BA
So Δp_A = −Δp_B
Hence p_A + p_B is unchanged

items.q: 5 kg gun, 0.01 kg bullet at 500 m/s: gun speed (m/s)
2 kg gun, 0.02 kg bullet at 300 m/s: gun speed (m/s)
Shell at rest splits: 1 kg at 30 m/s; other 2 kg speed (m/s)
Total momentum before an explosion of a body at rest
60 kg man jumps off 40 kg boat at 2 m/s: boat speed (m/s)

quiz.explain: 0 = 1 × 40 + 2 × v → v = −20 m s⁻¹, so its speed is 20 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction.
quiz.mistake: Uses the total mass 3 kg for the second piece

quiz.q: Momentum of a system is conserved when
options: The net external force on it is zero
quiz.explain: Internal forces cancel in pairs; only external forces can change total momentum.

quiz.q: A rocket moves forward in empty space because
options: It pushes exhaust gas backward and the gas pushes it forward
quiz.explain: Third law and momentum conservation: no air is needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rockets need air to push against

quiz.q: A shell moving horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ explodes into two equal halves. One half falls straight down with zero horizontal speed just after the explosion. The other half's horizontal speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Horizontal momentum: m × 10 = (m/2)(0) + (m/2)v → v = 20 m s⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each half keeps 10 m s⁻¹

quiz.q: When we walk, the force that pushes us forward is
options: Our muscles pushing on our own body
The ground's frictional push on our feet
quiz.explain: Our feet push the ground backward; the ground's reaction (static friction) pushes us forward.
quiz.mistake: Thinks internal muscle forces alone move the body

quiz.q: Two skaters at rest push each other apart. Skater A (40 kg) moves at 3 m s⁻¹. Skater B (60 kg) moves at (in m s⁻¹)
quiz.explain: 40 × 3 = 60 × v → v = 2 m s⁻¹, opposite to A.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The total momentum of a shell is unchanged just after it explodes in flight.
Reason (R): The forces of the explosion are internal to the shell–fragments system.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Internal forces cancel in pairs and gravity acts only negligibly during the brief explosion, so total momentum is conserved. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks rockets fly by pushing against air, so they shouldn't work in space. Explain using the third law and conservation of momentum.
teach.praise: The rocket throws gas back and the gas shoves the rocket forward. No air needed!
teach.nudge: What does the rocket push on? What stays the same for the rocket plus its gas?

topics.title: Equilibrium of a particle

learn.hook: A street lamp hangs perfectly still from two wires. The wires' pulls and the lamp's weight form a perfect closed triangle.
points: A particle is in equilibrium when the net external force on it is zero (it is at rest or moving uniformly).
Two forces in equilibrium must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction along the same line.
Three concurrent forces in equilibrium can be drawn head to tail as a closed triangle (triangle law of forces); many forces form a closed polygon.
Component conditions: ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣF_z = 0.
Method: draw the forces on the point (e.g. the knot), resolve them along x and y, and solve ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.

example.q: A 4 kg mass hangs from a string. A horizontal force F pulls the mass aside until the string makes θ with the vertical, where tan θ = 0.75. Find F and the tension (g = 10 m s⁻²).
steps: Vertical: T cos θ = mg = 40 N.

learn.reallife: Engineers designing the overhead electric lines for Indian Railways' electrified tracks balance the tensions and weights at every support point.

games.title: Solving an equilibrium problem
items: Choose the point or body in equilibrium
Draw all forces acting on it
Choose x and y axes
Resolve each force into components
Set ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 and solve

games.title: Equilibrium facts
items: A body moving with constant velocity is in equilibrium.
Net force is zero.
Two forces of 5 N and 7 N can keep a particle in equilibrium.
Two forces must be equal and opposite.
Three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when drawn head to tail.
Their resultant is zero.
A body at the top of its vertical throw is in equilibrium.
Gravity acts; net force is not zero.
Forces of 3 N, 4 N and 5 N can be in equilibrium.
They can form a closed 3-4-5 triangle.

quiz.q: Which set of three forces CANNOT keep a particle in equilibrium?
quiz.explain: Three forces can balance only if each is ≤ the sum of the other two. 7 > 2 + 3, so no closed triangle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any three forces can be arranged to balance

quiz.q: A 10 kg mass hangs at rest from a rope (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The tension in the rope in N is
quiz.explain: Equilibrium: T = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mass instead of the weight

quiz.q: A 20 kg mass hangs from two strings, each making 60° with the vertical (g = 10 m s⁻², cos 60° = 0.5). The tension in each string in N is
quiz.mistake: Assumes each string carries half the weight

quiz.q: A 6 kg mass hangs from a string and is pulled aside by a horizontal force till the string makes 45° with the vertical (g = 10 m s⁻²). The horizontal force in N is
quiz.explain: tan 45° = F/mg → F = mg = 60 N.

quiz.q: The conditions for equilibrium of a particle in component form are
quiz.explain: Every component of the net force must vanish.

quiz.q: Two forces acting on a particle keep it in equilibrium. They must be
options: Of any magnitude if they are opposite
Equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and along the same line
quiz.explain: Only then is their sum zero.

quiz.q: Forces of 3 N east and 4 N north act on a particle. The third force needed for equilibrium has magnitude (in N)
quiz.explain: It must cancel the resultant √(9 + 16) = 5 N, pointing south-west.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A lamp hanging from two wires is in equilibrium.
Reason (R): The vector sum of the two tensions and the weight is zero.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Zero net force is the meaning of equilibrium, and R gives it. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equilibrium needs no forces at all

teach.ask: Gappu is hanging from two twigs and wonders why he doesn't fall. Explain the conditions for equilibrium and how to find the tension in each twig.
teach.praise: My weight is balanced by the two pulls; the forces make a closed triangle. Safe and sound!
teach.nudge: What must the total force be? How do you find each tension using components?

topics.title: Common forces: gravity, normal, tension and spring

learn.hook: When you sit on a chair, the chair pushes up on you with exactly your weight. Where does that push come from? From electric forces between atoms!
points: Gravity acts at a distance; most other mechanical forces (normal, friction, tension, spring) are contact forces.
Normal reaction N is the component of contact force perpendicular to the surfaces in contact.
Tension acts along a string, pulling on the bodies attached; for a massless string it is the same throughout.
Spring force F = −kx: a restoring force proportional to extension or compression x, directed opposite to it (k is the spring constant).
Contact forces ultimately come from electrical forces between the charged particles (electrons and nuclei) of the surfaces.

example.q: A spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 5 cm. Find the restoring force.
steps: Magnitude 10 N, directed back towards the natural length.

learn.reallife: The shock absorbers of a motorbike and the spring balance at a sabzi mandi both rely on F = −kx.

games.title: Force ↔ description
pairs: Perpendicular to the surface of contact
Pull along a string or rope
Parallel to the surface of contact

quiz.q: A spring with k = 400 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.05 m. The magnitude of the spring force in N is
The negative sign in F = −kx shows that the spring force
options: Is opposite to the displacement from natural length
quiz.explain: It is a restoring force, always pointing back towards the natural length.
quiz.mistake: Reads the minus sign as a negative magnitude

quiz.q: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal table (g = 10 m s⁻²). The normal force on it in N is
quiz.explain: Vertical equilibrium: N = mg = 50 N.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mass instead of the weight

quiz.q: Contact forces like normal force and friction ultimately arise from
options: Electrical forces between charged constituents of matter
quiz.explain: Electrons and nuclei of the two surfaces interact electrically.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gravity between atoms is responsible

quiz.q: In a massless string passing over a frictionless pulley, the tension is
quiz.explain: A massless string needs no net force, so the tension is uniform.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pulley changes the tension

quiz.q: The normal force on a block on a surface is
options: Perpendicular to the surface of contact
quiz.explain: It is perpendicular to the surface; on an incline N = mg cos θ, not mg.
quiz.mistake: Thinks N is always equal to mg

quiz.q: A 2 kg block hangs from a spring of k = 196 N m⁻¹ and is at rest (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The extension in m is

Assertion (A): Friction and normal reaction are both components of the contact force between two surfaces.
Reason (R): Friction always acts in the direction of motion of a body.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: friction opposes relative motion (or impending motion) between the surfaces.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks the chair 'just sits there' and does nothing while he sits on it. Explain normal force, tension, spring force, and where contact forces come from.
teach.praise: The chair pushes me up with electric forces between atoms! And springs push back with kx.
teach.nudge: Which way does the chair push you, and why? What kind of force is behind all contact forces?

topics.title: Static, kinetic and rolling friction

learn.hook: Push a heavy almirah: nothing happens, then suddenly it jerks into motion. Static friction just gave up its maximum value.
points: Static friction f_s opposes impending relative motion. It is self-adjusting: it equals the applied force up to a limit f_s(max) = μ_s N.
Laws of friction: limiting friction is independent of the area of contact and proportional to the normal reaction N.
Kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N acts once sliding begins, opposing relative motion. μ_k < μ_s, and f_k is roughly independent of speed.
Angle of repose: a block on an incline is just about to slide when tan θ = μ_s.
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction; that's why wheels and ball bearings are used.

example.q: A 10 kg box rests on a floor with μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.4 (g = 10 m s⁻²). What friction acts if you push with (a) 30 N, (b) 60 N?
steps: (a) 30 N < 50 N: box stays; static friction = 30 N.
(b) 60 N > 50 N: box slides; kinetic friction = 0.4 × 100 = 40 N.

learn.reallife: Ball bearings in the wheels of Indian Railways' bogies replace sliding with rolling, saving huge amounts of energy.

games.title: Static or kinetic friction?
items: Box at rest, pushed gently
Feet on the ground while walking
Book sliding across a desk
Car tyres skidding with locked brakes
Block resting on a slope
Sledge gliding down a snowy hill

games.title: Laws of friction
items: Limiting friction depends on the area of contact.
It is independent of area.
μ_k is usually less than μ_s.
It is easier to keep a body sliding than to start it.
Static friction always equals μ_s N.
That is only its maximum; it adjusts up to that limit.
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
Hence wheels.
If tan θ of an incline exceeds μ_s, a block on it starts to slide.
θ exceeds the angle of repose.

quiz.q: The same crate (20 kg) is pushed with 50 N and does not move. The friction force on it in N is
quiz.explain: Static friction self-adjusts to match the 50 N push.
quiz.mistake: Assumes friction is always at its maximum

quiz.q: A block just begins to slide on an incline at 30°. The coefficient of static friction is (tan 30° = 0.577)
quiz.explain: At the angle of repose, μ_s = tan θ = 0.577.

quiz.q: A 5 kg block slides on a floor with μ_k = 0.2 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The kinetic friction in N is
Limiting friction between two surfaces is
options: Proportional to the normal reaction and independent of area of contact
Proportional to the area of contact
quiz.explain: These are the empirical laws of friction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bigger contact area means more friction

quiz.q: Why is it easier to keep a box sliding than to start it moving?
options: Normal force decreases when it moves
quiz.explain: Kinetic friction is smaller than limiting static friction.

quiz.q: A box slides with kinetic friction 40 N. Its speed doubles. The kinetic friction becomes approximately (in N)
quiz.explain: Kinetic friction is roughly independent of speed.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Ball bearings reduce friction in machines.
Reason (R): Ball bearings are usually made of hardened steel.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the material is not the reason; bearings work because rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true but irrelevant fact

teach.ask: Gappu pushes a pebble softly and it doesn't move, then pushes harder and it slides. He thinks friction 'switched on'. Explain static, kinetic and rolling friction.
teach.praise: Static friction matches my push up to μN, then kinetic friction (smaller) takes over. Rolling is easiest of all!
teach.nudge: Was friction there before the pebble moved? What is the most it can be? What changes after sliding starts?

topics.title: Friction at work: walking, trucks, connected blocks and lifts

learn.hook: Without friction you couldn't walk, a car couldn't move, and a lift ride would feel very strange. Let's put forces to work.
points: Friction is essential: static friction from the road drives a car forward and lets us walk. Lubricants and ball bearings reduce unwanted friction in machines.
A box on a truck floor (μ_s) stays put as long as the truck's acceleration a ≤ μ_s g, because static friction is the only horizontal force on the box.
Block m₁ on a table (μ_k) tied over a pulley to a hanging m₂: a = (m₂ − μ_k m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) and T = m₂(g − a).
Atwood machine (m₁ > m₂): a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂), T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
Lift: apparent weight N = m(g + a) when accelerating up, m(g − a) when accelerating down, 0 in free fall, and mg at constant velocity.

example.q: A 2 kg block on a table (μ_k = 0.1) is tied by a string over a pulley to a hanging 3 kg block (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find a and T.
steps: a = (m₂g − μ_k m₁g)/(m₁ + m₂) = (30 − 2)/5 = 5.6 m s⁻².
Hanging block: m₂g − T = m₂a → T = 3(10 − 5.6) = 13.2 N.
Check table block: T − 2 = 2 × 5.6 → T = 13.2 N ✓.

learn.reallife: Riding a lift at a Mumbai high-rise, you feel heavier as it starts upward and lighter as it starts downward: the normal force from the floor changes.

games.title: Lift motion ↔ apparent weight of 60 kg person (g = 10 m s⁻²)

50 kg in lift accelerating down at 1 m/s²: N (N)

quiz.explain: Static friction μ_s mg is the only horizontal force: a_max = μ_s g = 0.2 × 9.8 = 1.96 m s⁻².

quiz.q: A 70 kg man stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m s⁻² (g = 10 m s⁻²). The floor pushes him with (in N)
The same man in a lift moving down at constant speed has an apparent weight (in N) of
quiz.explain: Constant velocity means a = 0, so N = mg = 700 N.
quiz.mistake: Thinks downward motion reduces the reading

quiz.q: A 4 kg block on a frictionless table is tied over a pulley to a hanging 1 kg block (g = 10 m s⁻²). The acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 10/5 = 2 m s⁻².

quiz.q: What force actually makes a car accelerate forward on a road?
options: The engine pushing the car directly
Static friction from the road on the tyres
quiz.explain: The tyres push the road backward; the road's static friction pushes the car forward.
quiz.mistake: Thinks internal engine forces alone accelerate the car

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A person in a freely falling lift feels weightless.
Reason (R): In free fall, gravity stops acting on the person.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true because the floor's normal force becomes zero. R is false: gravity still acts; that is why the person falls.

teach.ask: Gappu is riding in a lift and feels heavy at the start and light near the top. Explain using N = m(g ± a), and why friction is needed to walk.
teach.praise: The floor pushes harder when the lift speeds up upward, and less when it speeds up downward. And friction lets me walk!
teach.nudge: What does the floor's push equal when the lift accelerates upward? Downward?

topics.title: Circular motion: centripetal force and level roads

learn.hook: A motorbike rider taking a sharp turn on a wet road skids out. The road's friction simply could not supply enough centripetal force.
points: Circular motion needs a net force towards the centre: f_c = mv²/R (the centripetal force).
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is supplied by existing forces: tension (stone on string), gravity (planets), friction (car on road), normal force (wall of death).
Car on a level road: static friction provides mv²/R, so mv²/R ≤ μ_s mg → v_max = √(μ_s R g), independent of mass.
Cyclist or car on a level turn: if v² > μ_s R g, it skids outward. Slow down or reduce sharpness (increase R).

example.q: A car takes a level turn of radius 20 m with μ_s = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). What is the maximum safe speed?

learn.reallife: Road signs on ghat roads of the Western Ghats warn of sharp curves because the friction available limits safe turning speed.

items.q: m = 2 kg, v = 4 m/s, R = 2 m: Fc (N)

quiz.q: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 1 m at 4 m s⁻¹. The tension (centripetal force) in N is
A cyclist goes round a level curve of radius 3 m at 5 m s⁻¹ with μ_s = 0.1 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Will he slip?
options: Yes, because v² = 25 exceeds μ_s R g = 2.94
No, because v² is less than μ_s R g
quiz.explain: Safe only if v² ≤ μ_s R g; 25 > 2.94, so friction cannot supply mv²/R.

quiz.q: The maximum safe speed on a level curve does not depend on
quiz.explain: v_max = √(μ_s R g); mass cancels.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heavier vehicles can go faster

quiz.q: For a car on a level road with μ_s = 0.6 and R = 60 m (g = 10 m s⁻²), v_max in m s⁻¹ is
Centripetal force is best described as
options: The net force towards the centre, provided by real forces such as tension or friction
A new force that appears in circular motion
quiz.explain: It is a role played by existing forces, not a separate force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks centripetal force is an extra force to add

quiz.q: A car of mass 1000 kg moves on a level circular road of radius 50 m at 10 m s⁻¹. The friction force needed in N is
quiz.mistake: Divides by v instead of squaring it

quiz.q: If the speed of a car on a curve is doubled, the friction force needed to keep it on the same curve becomes how many times the original?
quiz.explain: f = mv²/R ∝ v².

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A car can take a level curve at any speed if its tyres are new.
Reason (R): The static friction available cannot exceed μ_s mg.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: v_max = √(μ_s R g) limits the speed whatever the tyres. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 'centripetal force' is a mystery force that appears whenever things go round. Explain what really supplies it on a level road, and the speed limit.
teach.praise: Centripetal force is a job, not a new force! On a flat road, friction does the job, up to √(μRg).
teach.nudge: Which real force pulls the car towards the centre on a level road? Is there a speed limit?

topics.title: Banked roads: optimum and maximum safe speed

learn.hook: Ever noticed that the outer edge of a highway curve is raised? That tilt lets the road itself help steer the car.
points: On a road banked at θ, the normal force N tilts inward. Equations (friction f down the slope): N cos θ = mg + f sin θ and N sin θ + f cos θ = mv²/R.
With f ≤ μ_s N, the maximum safe speed is v_max = √[Rg(μ_s + tan θ)/(1 − μ_s tan θ)].
Optimum speed (no friction needed): v₀ = √(Rg tan θ). At this speed, wear on tyres is least.
Banking raises v_max above the level-road value √(μ_s R g), which is why race tracks and highway curves are banked.

example.q: A curve of radius 90 m is banked with tan θ = 1/3, and μ_s = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the optimum and maximum safe speeds.
example.answer: v₀ ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, v_max = 30 m s⁻¹

learn.reallife: Cycle velodromes have steeply banked tracks, and highway curves are gently banked, so that vehicles can corner faster and more safely than on flat ground.

Set friction to zero
Vertical: N cos θ = mg
Horizontal: N sin θ = mv²/R

At v₀ no friction is needed.

v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) has no mass.

The horizontal component of the normal force

quiz.mistake: Thinks heavier cars need different banking

teach.ask: Gappu asks why highway curves are tilted, and what speed a car should go so it doesn't even need friction. Explain banking.
teach.praise: The tilt makes the normal force lean in and do the turning. At √(Rg tan θ), no friction needed at all!
teach.nudge: Which force leans inward on a banked road? What is the speed at which friction is not needed?

topics.title: Solving mechanics problems with free-body diagrams

learn.hook: Most mistakes in mechanics come from one thing: forgetting a force or adding one that isn't there. Free-body diagrams fix that.
points: Step 1: draw a schematic diagram showing all bodies, supports and connections (strings, pulleys, springs).
Step 2: choose a convenient part as your system and draw its free-body diagram (FBD) showing only that body.
Step 3: show all EXTERNAL forces on it (weight, normal, tension, friction, applied), known and unknown, with directions. Do not include forces the body exerts on others.
Step 4: apply F = ma to the chosen system. When switching to another body, use the third law for the force between them.
Example: block B (3 kg) resting on block A (5 kg) on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²): B pushes A down with 30 N; the floor pushes A up with 80 N.

example.q: A 3 kg block B rests on a 5 kg block A, which rests on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the forces on A.
steps: FBD of B: weight 30 N down, normal from A 30 N up.
Third law: B pushes A down with 30 N.
FBD of A: weight 50 N down, 30 N down from B, floor's normal N up.
example.answer: 30 N down from B, 50 N weight, 80 N up from floor

learn.reallife: IIT JEE toppers swear by one habit: draw the FBD before writing any equation. It works just as well for your CBSE paper.

quiz.explain: Horse–cart forces are internal. The ground's forces are external.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to find the push between two boxes being shoved across the floor, but keeps adding the wrong forces. Teach him the four-step free-body method.
teach.praise: Isolate one box, draw only forces ON it, apply F = ma, then use the third law for the next box. So tidy!
teach.nudge: Which forces go in the diagram of one box? How do you move from one box to the other?

topics.title: The scalar (dot) product

learn.hook: A coolie carrying a heavy bag on his head across a level platform is tired, yet in physics he did zero work on the bag. The dot product explains why.
points: In everyday language 'work', 'energy' and 'power' are loose words; in physics they have exact definitions built on the scalar product.
Scalar (dot) product: A·B = AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between A and B. The result is a scalar.
Properties: commutative (A·B = B·A) and distributive (A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C).
Unit vectors: î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1 and î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0.
Component form: A·B = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y + A_zB_z.

example.q: Find A·B for A = 2î + 3ĵ − k̂ and B = 4î − ĵ + 2k̂.

learn.reallife: Solar panel installers in Rajasthan tilt panels so that the sunlight direction and the panel's normal have the largest dot product, maximising captured energy.

quiz.mistake: Confuses dot product with cross product

quiz.mistake: Treats it like a cross product

quiz.mistake: Thinks a zero product needs a zero vector

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but commutativity does not explain A·A = A²; that follows from cos 0° = 1.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true property as the reason

quiz.q: Riya says she did a lot of 'work' by reading notes for two hours at her desk. In physics, work is done on a body only when
options: A force acts on it and its point of application moves with a component of displacement along the force
A person feels tired after an activity
A lot of time is spent on a task
Any force acts on it, even if nothing moves
quiz.explain: In physics, work W = F·d needs a force and a displacement with a component along it. Everyday 'work' (reading, effort, tiredness) is not physics work.
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday meaning of 'work' instead of the physics definition

teach.ask: Gappu thinks multiplying two vectors always gives another vector. Explain the dot product, its formula and how to compute it from components.
teach.praise: So the dot product is just a number: AB cos θ, or multiply matching components and add!
teach.nudge: What kind of answer does a dot product give? How does the angle come in?

topics.title: Work done by a constant force

learn.hook: Pulling a suitcase by its handle at an angle: only the part of your pull along the floor does work.
points: Angle between vectors: cos θ = A·B/(AB).
Component of F along d = F·d/|d| = F cos θ.
Work by a constant force: W = F·d = Fd cos θ. It is a scalar; SI unit joule (1 J = 1 N m).

Zero work in three cases: no displacement (pushing a wall), no force (a body moving uniformly in free space), or force perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°: coolie carrying a load horizontally, gravity on a body moving horizontally).

example.q: F = 2î + ĵ + 2k̂ N and d = 2î − 2ĵ + k̂ m. Find the work done and the angle between F and d.

learn.reallife: Porters at Indian railway stations do zero work (in physics) on a head-load while walking on the level, but plenty of work while climbing the stairs to the foot-over-bridge.

teach.nudge: What does work depend on besides force? What if the rock never moves?

topics.title: Positive and negative work, and units of energy

learn.hook: When you lower a heavy suitcase from a train's upper berth, gravity does positive work and your hands do negative work.
points: 0° ≤ θ < 90°: W > 0 (force helps motion). 90° < θ ≤ 180°: W < 0 (force opposes motion).
Kinetic friction opposes relative motion, so it does negative work on a sliding body.
Units of work and energy: joule (J); erg = 10⁻⁷ J; electron volt eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; kilowatt hour kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; calorie = 4.186 J.
Net work = sum of works by all forces (each with its sign).

example.q: A 50 N push moves a box 5 m on a floor where friction is 20 N. Find the work done by each force and the net work.

learn.reallife: Your electricity bill counts energy in 'units', and 1 unit = 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. A 2 kW geyser running for 30 minutes uses 1 unit.

quiz.explain: Gravity (down) opposes the displacement (up), θ = 180°.

quiz.explain: Force opposite to displacement means θ = 180°, so W < 0. R explains A.

teach.nudge: What happens to the sign of work when the force opposes the motion? What units of energy do you know?

topics.title: Kinetic energy and the work–energy theorem

learn.hook: A raindrop falling from a cloud a kilometre up should hit you at over 140 m s⁻¹. It doesn't, because air resistance does a lot of negative work.
points: Start with v² − u² = 2as and multiply by m/2: ½mv² − ½mu² = mas = Fs.
Kinetic energy K = ½mv² (a scalar, never negative).
Work–energy theorem: the change in kinetic energy equals the net work done by all forces: K_f − K_i = W_net.
Typical kinetic energies span a huge range: a falling raindrop ~10⁻³ J, a running person ~10³ J, a car on a highway ~10⁵–10⁶ J.

example.q: A 2 g raindrop falls 500 m and lands at 20 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the work done by gravity and by air resistance.

learn.reallife: A Vande Bharat train of about 4 × 10⁵ kg at 30 m s⁻¹ carries nearly 2 × 10⁸ J of kinetic energy, which its brakes must remove to stop.

So ΔK = work done

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: A is false: only the speed stays constant; the direction can change (as in uniform circular motion). R is true.

quiz.mistake: Has no feel for the size of kinetic energies of everyday objects

topics.title: Work done by a variable force

learn.hook: Stretching a resistance band at the gym gets harder the further you pull. You can't just use W = Fd here.
points: For a force that changes with position, break the displacement into small steps Δx where F is nearly constant: W ≈ Σ F(x)Δx.
In the limit Δx → 0: W = ∫ F(x) dx from x_i to x_f.
Graphically, work done = area under the force–displacement (F–x) graph; area below the x-axis is negative work.
Use simple shapes (rectangles, triangles, trapeziums) to find areas for piecewise-linear graphs.

example.q: A woman pushes a trunk with 100 N for the first 10 m; then her push falls linearly to 50 N over the next 10 m. Find the work done by her.

learn.reallife: Engineers testing car crash barriers at the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune, find the energy absorbed from the area under force–crush graphs.

topics.title: Work–energy theorem for variable forces and its uses

learn.hook: A bullet punching through a plank loses most of its energy in a split second. The work–energy theorem tells you how much without knowing the messy force.
points: Proof for a variable force: dK/dt = mv dv/dt = Fv = F dx/dt, so dK = F dx. Integrating, K_f − K_i = ∫F dx = W.
The theorem is the integral form of Newton's second law. It is a scalar equation (no direction needed) and holds in inertial frames.
It is powerful when the force is complicated: you only need the work.
Bullet through a plank: kinetic energy lost = work done by the plank's resistance. Block entering a rough region: K_f = K_i + W_friction (W_friction < 0).

example.q: A 20 g bullet enters a plank at 300 m s⁻¹ and emerges at 100 m s⁻¹. Find the kinetic energy lost and the fraction lost.

learn.reallife: Bulletproof jackets used by the CRPF are tested by how much kinetic energy their layers absorb, which is the work done against the bullet.

topics.title: Potential energy and conservative forces

learn.hook: Water held behind the Bhakra Dam stores energy simply because of where it is. Release it and the turbines spin.
points: Potential energy is stored energy due to position or configuration (a raised stone, a stretched bow).
Near the Earth's surface, gravitational PE V = mgh (taking V = 0 at the reference level). In 1D, F = −dV/dx (force points towards lower PE).
A force is conservative if the work done by it depends only on the initial and final positions (not on the path), and is zero over any closed path. Gravity and spring force are conservative.
Friction is non-conservative: its work depends on the path and is not zero over a closed path, so no potential energy can be defined for it.
PE has the same dimensions [M L² T⁻²] and unit (joule) as kinetic energy.

example.q: A 2 kg stone is raised 5 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find its gain in PE, and show F = −dV/dx gives its weight.
steps: The minus sign means the force points downward (towards lower V).

learn.reallife: In pumped-storage plants like Tehri, water is pumped uphill at night (storing PE) and released through turbines during peak demand.

items: Work done by gravity in taking a body around a closed loop is zero.
Gravity is conservative.
Work done by friction depends on the path taken.
Longer path, more negative work.
Potential energy can be defined for friction.
Only for conservative forces.
F = −dV/dx means force points towards decreasing potential energy.
Bodies tend to move to lower PE.
Potential energy and kinetic energy have different dimensions.
Both are [M L² T⁻²].

quiz.q: A 5 kg body is lifted 4 m (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its gain in gravitational potential energy in J is
A force is conservative if the work done by it
options: Depends only on the initial and final positions
quiz.explain: Path-independence (and zero work round a closed path) defines a conservative force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks conservative means zero work always

quiz.q: Which force is non-conservative?
quiz.explain: Friction's work depends on path and converts energy to heat.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every natural force is conservative

quiz.q: V(x) = 3x² J (x in m). The force on the particle at x = 2 m in N is
A ball is carried from the ground to a shelf 2 m high by two different routes. The work done by gravity is
quiz.explain: Gravity is conservative: W = −mgh, path-independent.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a longer path means more work by gravity

quiz.q: The SI unit of potential energy is
quiz.explain: Like all energy, PE is in joules.
quiz.mistake: Confuses energy with power or force

quiz.q: A block is dragged around a closed path on a rough floor and returned to its start. The total work done by friction is
quiz.explain: Friction opposes motion everywhere along the path; the works add up negatively.
quiz.mistake: Applies the closed-path rule to friction

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Potential energy cannot be defined for kinetic friction.
Reason (R): The work done by friction depends on the path followed.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: PE requires work to depend only on end points; friction fails this. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every force has a PE

teach.ask: Gappu asks why we talk about 'gravitational potential energy' but never 'friction potential energy'. Explain PE and conservative forces.
teach.praise: PE is stored by position, and only conservative forces like gravity get one. Friction just wastes energy as heat!
teach.nudge: What makes a force conservative? Does friction's work depend on the path?

topics.title: Conservation of mechanical energy

learn.hook: A coconut falling from a 20 m palm tree trades potential energy for kinetic energy all the way down. The total? Unchanged.
points: If only conservative forces act, total mechanical energy E = K + V remains constant.
Derivation: for a conservative force, W = −ΔV; by the work–energy theorem W = ΔK. So ΔK = −ΔV, i.e. Δ(K + V) = 0.
Ball dropped from height H: at height h, V = mgh and K = mg(H − h); just before the ground, K = mgH and v = √(2gH).
With friction or air resistance, mechanical energy is not conserved: some becomes heat.

example.q: A 1 kg coconut falls from a 20 m tree (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find its kinetic energy and speed at 5 m above the ground.

learn.reallife: A child on a swing at a village fair keeps converting PE at the ends to KE at the bottom; friction and air drag slowly steal energy, so someone has to keep pushing.

games.title: Energy of a ball dropped from H (no air)
games.prompt: Arrange from release to just before impact
items: At release: all PE (mgH), K = 0
At H/2: PE = KE = mgH/2
Just above ground: nearly all KE
At ground: K = mgH, v = √(2gH)

items.q: Drop from 5 m: speed at ground (m/s)
Drop from 20 m: speed at ground (m/s)
2 kg from 10 m: KE at ground (J)
2 kg from 10 m: KE at 4 m height (J)
Thrown up at 10 m/s: max height (m)

quiz.q: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 45 m (g = 10 m s⁻², no air resistance). Its speed just before hitting the ground in m s⁻¹ is
For the same ball (2 kg from 45 m), its kinetic energy at a height of 25 m in J is
quiz.mistake: Uses the current height instead of the drop

quiz.q: Mechanical energy is conserved when
quiz.explain: Non-conservative forces like friction change mechanical energy into heat.
quiz.mistake: Thinks energy is conserved in every situation as mechanical energy

quiz.q: At what height above the ground is the KE of a falling ball equal to its PE, if dropped from 40 m?
quiz.explain: K = V means mgh = mg(40 − h) → h = 20 m.
quiz.mistake: Picks a quarter of the height

quiz.q: The derivation of energy conservation uses
options: ΔK = W (work–energy theorem) and W = −ΔV (conservative force)
quiz.explain: Combining the two gives Δ(K + V) = 0.

quiz.q: A pendulum bob is released from 0.45 m above its lowest point (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its speed at the lowest point in m s⁻¹ is
A ball thrown up at 20 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²) reaches a maximum height (in m) of
quiz.explain: At the top K = 0: ½mv² = mgh → h = v²/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A ball dropped from a height reaches the ground with the same speed whatever its mass (ignoring air).
Reason (R): A heavier ball experiences a larger gravitational force.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but R alone doesn't explain A; the larger force is balanced by larger inertia, so mass cancels in mgh = ½mv².
quiz.mistake: Takes a true but incomplete fact as the explanation

teach.ask: Gappu drops a nut from a branch and wonders where its energy goes. Explain conservation of mechanical energy, and when it fails.
teach.praise: PE turns into KE, but K + V stays the same if only gravity acts. Friction would spoil the party!
teach.nudge: What stays constant as the nut falls? When does that rule stop working?

topics.title: Vertical circles and potential-energy graphs

learn.hook: A 'loop-the-loop' ride at an amusement park is designed so the car is fast enough at the top. Energy conservation decides how fast it must be at the bottom.
points: Bob on a string of length L in a vertical circle: at the top, tension ≥ 0 needs mv_t²/L ≥ mg, so v_top(min) = √(gL).
Energy conservation between bottom and top (height 2L): v_b² = v_t² + 4gL. So v_bottom(min) = √(5gL).
With v_b = √(5gL): tension at the bottom = mg + mv_b²/L = 6mg; tension at the top = 0.
Potential-energy graph: K = E − V(x) ≥ 0. Regions where V(x) > E are forbidden; the particle turns back where V = E (turning points).

example.q: A 0.2 kg bob on a 1 m string must just complete a vertical circle (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the minimum speeds at the top and bottom.

learn.reallife: Stunt riders in a 'maut ka kuan' (wall of death) at Indian melas must keep their speed above a minimum, or gravity wins.

games.title: Deriving v_bottom(min) = √(5gL)
items: At the top, tension can just become zero
Then mg = mv_t²/L, so v_t² = gL
Energy: ½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + mg(2L)
v_b² = gL + 4gL = 5gL
v_b = √(5gL)

games.title: Vertical circles and PE graphs
items: At the minimum speed, the tension at the top of the circle is zero.
Gravity alone provides the centripetal force.
Minimum speed at the bottom to complete the loop is √(2gL).
It is √(5gL).
A particle can be found where its potential energy exceeds its total energy.
That would need negative K.
Turning points occur where V(x) = E.
K = 0 there.
Tension is greatest at the lowest point of a vertical circle.
There T must also balance the weight.

quiz.q: A stone on a 0.9 m string just completes a vertical circle (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its speed at the top in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: v_top = √(gL) = √9 = 3 m s⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the speed at the top can be zero for a string

quiz.q: For the same stone (L = 0.9 m), the minimum speed at the bottom in m s⁻¹ is (√45 ≈ 6.71)
A 0.5 kg bob moves in a vertical circle with the minimum speed needed. The tension at the bottom (g = 10 m s⁻²) in N is
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add mg to mv²/L

quiz.q: Why can't the bob on a string have zero speed at the top of the circle?
options: The string would go slack because gravity needs a speed of at least √(gL) to keep it moving in the circle
quiz.explain: Tension cannot be negative; at the top mg ≤ mv²/L must hold.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a rod and a string behave the same

quiz.q: A particle has total energy E = 5 J. Its potential energy is V = 8 J at x = 2 m. At x = 2 m, the particle
quiz.explain: K = E − V = −3 J, impossible. That region is forbidden.
quiz.mistake: Takes the magnitude of E − V

quiz.q: On a PE graph, a particle with energy E turns back at points where
quiz.explain: At turning points K = 0, so V = E.
quiz.mistake: Thinks turning points are at the minimum of V

quiz.q: A bob on a 2 m string has speed √(5gL) at the bottom (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its speed at the side (height L) in m s⁻¹ is (√60 ≈ 7.75)
quiz.explain: v² = 5gL − 2gL = 3gL = 60, so v ≈ 7.75 m s⁻¹.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For a bob just completing a vertical circle on a string, the tension at the top is zero.
Reason (R): At the top, the weight alone can provide the required centripetal force mv²/L.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With v_top = √(gL), mg = mv²/L exactly, so T = 0. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tension is largest at the top

teach.ask: Gappu whirls a berry on a vine in a vertical circle and it keeps flopping at the top. Explain the minimum speeds using energy conservation.
teach.praise: √(gL) at the top, √(5gL) at the bottom. No more floppy berries!
teach.nudge: What speed is needed at the top so the vine stays tight? How does energy connect top and bottom?

topics.title: Spring potential energy

learn.hook: Railway platforms end in spring buffers. A slow-moving coach that overshoots is stopped by a spring that stores its kinetic energy.
points: Spring force (Hooke's law): F = −kx, where k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹) and x is the extension or compression.
Work done in stretching from 0 to x = area of triangle under the F–x line = ½kx².
Spring PE: V = ½kx². The spring force is conservative (work depends only on start and end x).
Energy swaps between ½mv² and ½kx²: speed is maximum at x = 0 (equilibrium), v_max = x_m √(k/m).
Car hitting a spring: ½mv² = ½kx_m²; with friction μ, ½mv² = ½kx_m² + μmg x_m.

example.q: A 1000 kg car hits a spring buffer (k = 16000 N m⁻¹) at 4 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum compression (ignore friction).

learn.reallife: Scooter suspensions and the bogie springs of a Rajdhani coach store and release elastic potential energy with every bump.

items.q: k = 100 N/m, x_m = 0.2 m, m = 1 kg: v_max (m/s)

quiz.q: A spring with k = 500 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 4 cm. The potential energy stored in J is
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert cm to m or square x

quiz.q: The spring constant k of a spring that stores 2 J when stretched by 0.1 m is (in N m⁻¹)
A 1000 kg car hits a spring buffer of k = 25000 N m⁻¹ at 5 m s⁻¹. The maximum compression in m is
quiz.explain: ½mv² = 12500 J = ½kx² → x² = 1 → x = 1 m.

quiz.q: Same car (1000 kg, 4 m s⁻¹) hits a spring of k = 44000 N m⁻¹ on a road with μ = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The maximum compression (solve 22000x² + 5000x − 8000 = 0) in m is
A 0.5 kg block on a spring (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m on a frictionless floor. Its maximum speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.mistake: Uses k/m without the square root

quiz.q: The spring force is conservative because
options: The work it does depends only on the initial and final extensions
quiz.explain: W = −(½kx_f² − ½kx_i²), independent of the path.
quiz.mistake: Thinks variable forces cannot be conservative

quiz.q: A block attached to a spring moves fastest
quiz.explain: There all the energy is kinetic (V = 0).
quiz.mistake: Thinks speed is greatest where force is greatest

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The work done in stretching a spring by x from its natural length is ½kx².
Reason (R): The spring force increases linearly from 0 to kx, so the work is the area of a triangle.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × x × kx = ½kx². R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Uses F × x with the final force, getting kx²

teach.ask: Gappu squeezed a spring and it shot his berry across the forest. Explain spring force, spring potential energy and where the speed is maximum.
teach.praise: ½kx² stored, then turned into kinetic energy, fastest at the natural length. Berry launcher!
teach.nudge: How much energy does a spring store? Where does the attached mass move fastest?

topics.title: Power

learn.hook: Two students climb the same stairs. Same work, but the one who sprints up uses more power. Power is about speed of doing work.
points: Average power P = W/t; instantaneous power P = dW/dt.
Since dW = F·dr, P = F·v.
SI unit: watt (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W.
Kilowatt hour (kWh) is a unit of ENERGY: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
Lifting a load at constant speed against friction: P = (mg + f)v.

example.q: A 1000 kg lift moves up at constant 3 m s⁻¹ against a friction force of 2000 N (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the motor's power.

learn.reallife: BEE star labels on Indian ACs and fridges compare power ratings and yearly energy use in kWh to show which appliance saves more electricity.

quiz.q: A boy of mass 50 kg climbs 6 m of stairs in 10 s (g = 10 m s⁻²). His average power in W is
A car engine exerts 2000 N while the car moves at 25 m s⁻¹. The power in kW is
The kilowatt hour is a unit of
quiz.explain: kW × h = (J/s) × s = J, so it measures energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'kilowatt' in the name makes it a power unit

quiz.q: A 1.5 kW geyser runs for 40 minutes a day. The energy used in kWh per day is
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by minutes instead of hours

quiz.q: A 1800 kg elevator carries a load upward at 2 m s⁻¹ against 4000 N friction (g = 10 m s⁻²). The minimum power in kW is
Instantaneous power delivered by a force F to a body moving with velocity v is
quiz.explain: P = dW/dt = F·dr/dt = F·v.

quiz.q: A motor of 1 hp runs for 1 hour. The energy used in kWh is (1 hp = 746 W)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert W to kW

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two cranes lifting identical loads to the same height do equal work, but the faster one has more power.
Reason (R): Power is the total work done by a machine.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: power is the rate of doing work, not the total work.

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'My sister and I both carried water up the hill, so we used the same power.' But she was twice as fast. Explain power.
teach.praise: Same work, but she did it in half the time, so double the power! Power is how fast work is done.
teach.nudge: Is power about how much work, or how fast? What is its unit?

topics.title: Collisions: elastic, inelastic and perfectly inelastic

learn.hook: When two kabaddi players crash and grab each other, they move off together. Momentum survives the crash; kinetic energy doesn't.
points: In every collision where external forces are negligible during the brief impact, total momentum is conserved.
Elastic collision: total kinetic energy is also conserved (e.g. ideal billiard balls, atomic collisions). Inelastic: some KE is converted to heat, sound or deformation.
Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together. Common velocity v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂).
KE lost in a perfectly inelastic collision: ΔK = ½ [m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)] (u₁ − u₂)².
Total energy is always conserved; it is only kinetic energy that may not be.

example.q: A 2 kg trolley at 6 m s⁻¹ hits a 1 kg trolley at rest and they stick. Find the common velocity and the KE lost.

learn.reallife: Railway wagons coupling in a shunting yard are a perfectly inelastic collision: they move off together and some kinetic energy becomes sound and heat.

games.title: Elastic or inelastic?
items: Two ideal steel balls bouncing off each other
Collision between gas molecules
A bullet embedding in a block
Two cars crumpling in a crash
Mud ball sticking to a wall
Neutron bouncing off a nucleus without exciting it

games.title: Collision truths
items: Momentum is conserved in an inelastic collision (no external force).
Always, if external impulse is negligible.
Kinetic energy is conserved in every collision.
Only in elastic collisions.
In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies move together afterwards.
They stick.
Total energy is lost in an inelastic collision.
Total energy is conserved; KE changes form.
A bob released from a height that hits an identical bob at rest elastically comes to rest.
Equal masses exchange velocities.

quiz.q: A 3 kg ball at 4 m s⁻¹ collides with and sticks to a 1 kg ball at rest. The common velocity in m s⁻¹ is
For the same collision (3 kg at 4 m s⁻¹ sticking to 1 kg at rest), the kinetic energy lost in J is
quiz.explain: K_i = 24 J; K_f = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J; loss = 6 J.

quiz.q: Which quantity is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system?
quiz.explain: With no external impulse, momentum is always conserved.

quiz.q: A 0.01 kg bullet at 500 m s⁻¹ embeds in a 0.99 kg block at rest. The block's speed after impact in m s⁻¹ is
In an elastic collision
options: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
quiz.explain: That is the definition of an elastic collision.

quiz.q: Two bodies of 1 kg each move towards each other at 2 m s⁻¹ each and stick. The KE lost in J is
quiz.explain: Total momentum = 0, so they stop; all 4 J of KE is lost.

quiz.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the kinetic energy lost is greatest when
options: The final common velocity is zero (total momentum zero)
quiz.explain: If total momentum is zero, the bodies stop and all KE is lost.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a body at rest maximises the loss

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In an inelastic collision, total momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy is not.
Reason (R): Some kinetic energy is converted into heat, sound or deformation, while no external impulse acts.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: R explains both parts of A: no external impulse (momentum) and conversion of KE.

teach.ask: Gappu bumped into a sparrow mid-air and they flew off together, slower. He thinks energy was destroyed. Explain types of collisions and what is conserved.
teach.praise: Momentum always survives; KE turns into heat and sound when we stick. Energy isn't destroyed, just changed!
teach.nudge: What is always conserved in a collision? What happens to the 'lost' kinetic energy?

topics.title: Elastic collisions in one dimension and neutron moderators

learn.hook: Nuclear reactors in Kudankulam use water to slow down fast neutrons. Why water and not lead? One-dimensional collisions explain it.
points: For m₁ moving at u₁ hitting m₂ at rest elastically: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂).
Equal masses: v₁ = 0, v₂ = u₁. They exchange velocities.
Heavy hits light (m₁ ≫ m₂): v₁ ≈ u₁, v₂ ≈ 2u₁. Light hits heavy (m₁ ≪ m₂): v₁ ≈ −u₁ (bounces back), v₂ ≈ 0.
Moderator: a neutron loses most KE when it hits a nucleus of similar mass. Fraction of KE kept = [(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)]². With deuterium (2m) it keeps 1/9; with carbon (12m) it keeps (11/13)² ≈ 0.72.

example.q: A 2 kg ball at 6 m s⁻¹ collides elastically head-on with a 1 kg ball at rest. Find the final velocities.
steps: Check KE: 36 J before; ½·2·4 + ½·1·64 = 4 + 32 = 36 J ✓.
example.answer: v₁ = 2 m s⁻¹, v₂ = 8 m s⁻¹

learn.reallife: India's pressurised heavy-water reactors (PHWRs), like those at Rawatbhata, use heavy water (deuterium) as the moderator.

games.title: Elastic collision case ↔ result
pairs: Very heavy hits very light at rest
Very light hits very heavy at rest
Light one bounces back at about u₁

items.q: Neutron on deuteron: fraction of KE lost

quiz.q: A 1 kg ball at 3 m s⁻¹ hits an identical ball at rest elastically. The speed of the second ball afterwards in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Equal masses exchange velocities: v₂ = 3 m s⁻¹, v₁ = 0.

quiz.q: A 4 kg body at 5 m s⁻¹ collides elastically with a 1 kg body at rest. The velocity of the 4 kg body after collision in m s⁻¹ is
For the same collision (4 kg at 5 m s⁻¹, 1 kg at rest), the velocity of the 1 kg body in m s⁻¹ is
A ping-pong ball hits a stationary bowling ball elastically. The ping-pong ball
options: Bounces back with nearly the same speed
Moves on at twice the speed
quiz.explain: m₁ ≪ m₂: v₁ ≈ −u₁, v₂ ≈ 0.

quiz.q: A neutron collides head-on elastically with a deuteron (mass 2m) at rest. The fraction of its kinetic energy it loses is
quiz.explain: It keeps [(m − 2m)/(m + 2m)]² = 1/9, so loses 8/9.

quiz.q: Why are light nuclei (like hydrogen or deuterium) good moderators?
options: Neutrons transfer most of their KE to nuclei of similar mass
quiz.explain: Energy transfer is greatest when masses are nearly equal.

quiz.q: A 1 kg ball at 6 m s⁻¹ hits a 2 kg ball at rest elastically. The velocity of the 1 kg ball after collision in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: v₁ = (1 − 2) × 6/3 = −2 m s⁻¹: it bounces back.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a head-on elastic collision of two equal masses with one at rest, the moving body stops.
Reason (R): With m₁ = m₂, v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂) = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The formula gives v₁ = 0 and v₂ = u₁. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu's teacher said reactors slow neutrons using water, not heavy lead blocks. Gappu is confused. Explain 1D elastic collisions and the moderator idea.
teach.praise: Hitting something of similar mass steals the most energy. Lead would just bounce the neutron back!
teach.nudge: What happens when equal masses collide elastically? Why does mass matter for slowing neutrons?

topics.title: Collisions in two dimensions

learn.hook: On a carrom board, the striker hits a coin off-centre and both fly away at an angle. Momentum is conserved along x and y separately.
points: In 2D, conserve momentum along each axis: m₁u₁ = m₁v₁ cos θ₁ + m₂v₂ cos θ₂ and 0 = m₁v₁ sin θ₁ − m₂v₂ sin θ₂ (target at rest, angles on opposite sides).
With the KE equation for elastic collisions, there are 3 equations but 4 unknowns (v₁, v₂, θ₁, θ₂), so one quantity (e.g. an angle) must be given.
Equal masses, elastic, one at rest: the two final velocities are perpendicular, θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
Billiards: if the cue ball is deflected by 37°, the target ball moves off at 53° on the other side.

example.q: A billiard ball hits an identical ball at rest elastically and is deflected by 30°. At what angle does the target ball move?
steps: Equal masses, elastic, target at rest: θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
θ₂ = 90° − 30° = 60°, on the other side of the original line.

learn.reallife: Snooker players use the 90° rule: when the cue ball (without spin) hits an identical object ball glancingly, the two balls separate at nearly right angles.

games.title: Solving a 2D collision
items: Choose x along the initial velocity
Write momentum conservation along x
Write momentum conservation along y
If elastic, write KE conservation
Use the given angle or speed to solve

games.title: 2D collision facts
items: In a 2D collision, momentum is conserved separately along x and y.
Momentum is a vector.
For equal masses in an elastic glancing collision (one at rest), the balls move off at 90° to each other.
θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
A 2D elastic collision can always be solved without any extra information.
3 equations, 4 unknowns.
In a 2D collision the y-momentum after collision is non-zero if the initial motion was along x.
Total y-momentum stays zero.
If equal balls collide elastically and one deflects at 40°, the other moves at 50°.
They add to 90°.

quiz.q: A ball hits an identical ball at rest elastically and moves off at 37° to its original direction. The other ball moves off at
quiz.explain: θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°, so θ₂ = 53°.

quiz.q: A 2 kg ball moving at 5 m s⁻¹ along x collides with a ball at rest. Afterwards, the total momentum along x in kg m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Momentum along x is conserved: 2 × 5 = 10 kg m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: A ball moving along the x-axis strikes a ball at rest, and both fly off at angles to the x-axis. The total momentum along y after the collision is
quiz.explain: Initially there was no y-momentum, so the y-components cancel afterwards.

quiz.q: In a 2D elastic collision, why is one extra piece of information (like an angle) needed?
options: There are only three equations for four unknowns
quiz.explain: Two momentum components and one energy equation cannot fix four unknowns.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the equations are always enough

quiz.q: A 1 kg ball at 4 m s⁻¹ (along x) hits an identical ball at rest. After an elastic collision, the first moves at 2 m s⁻¹ at 60° to x. The x-component of the second ball's velocity in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: x-momentum: 4 = 2 cos 60° + vₓ → vₓ = 4 − 1 = 3 m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: A 2 kg ball moving along x hits a 1 kg ball at rest. Afterwards the 1 kg ball moves along +y at 2 m s⁻¹. The y-component of the 2 kg ball's momentum in kg m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: Total y-momentum stays zero: p_y + 1 × 2 = 0, so p_y = −2 kg m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Momentum in a 2D collision is conserved
options: As a vector, so along each axis separately
Only if the collision is elastic
quiz.explain: Momentum is a vector; each component is conserved independently.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only the magnitude is conserved

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two identical balls, one at rest, separate at right angles after an elastic glancing collision.
Reason (R): Momentum and kinetic energy conservation for equal masses give v₁·v₂ = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: u₁ = v₁ + v₂ and u₁² = v₁² + v₂² together give v₁·v₂ = 0. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the angle depends on the speed

teach.ask: Gappu watched a carrom striker hit a coin off-centre and both shot away at an angle. Explain how momentum works in 2D and the 90° rule.
teach.praise: Momentum is conserved along x and y separately, and equal balls fly off at 90°. Collisions are pure physics!
teach.nudge: How is momentum conserved when things fly off at angles? What special angle appears for equal masses?

chapters.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

topics.title: Rigid bodies and the kinds of motion

learn.hook: A rolling cricket ball, a spinning ceiling fan and a car on a highway: one translates, one rotates, one does both. Rigid-body physics handles all three.
points: An extended body is a system of particles. A rigid body is an idealisation in which the distances between all pairs of particles stay fixed.
Pure translation: every particle has the same velocity at every instant (a block sliding down an incline).
Rotation about a fixed axis: every particle moves in a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis, with its centre on the axis (ceiling fan, potter's wheel).
Rotation about a fixed point (not a fixed axis): e.g. a spinning top whose axis itself swings around a vertical line (precession).
General motion of a rigid body = translation (of a reference point, like the centre of mass) + rotation about an axis through it (a rolling wheel).

example.q: A cylinder rolls down an incline without slipping. Is its motion pure translation?
steps: Points at the top, centre and bottom of the cylinder have different velocities at the same instant.
So it cannot be pure translation.
It is translation of the centre plus rotation about the axis through the centre.

learn.reallife: A giant wheel at a Dussehra mela rotates about a fixed axis, while a bullock-cart wheel on a village road both translates and rotates.

games.title: Type of motion
items: Block sliding down a smooth incline
Lift moving up a shaft
Ceiling fan
Potter's wheel
Bicycle wheel moving on a road
Rolling cricket ball

games.title: Rigid-body facts
items: In a rigid body, distances between particles do not change.
That is the definition.
In pure translation, different particles can have different velocities.
All particles share the same velocity.
In fixed-axis rotation, each particle moves in a circle centred on the axis.
In a plane perpendicular to the axis.
A spinning top that precesses rotates about a fixed axis.
It rotates about a fixed point; its axis moves.
Real bodies are perfectly rigid.
Rigid body is an idealisation; real bodies deform slightly.

quiz.q: A rigid body is one in which
options: All particles move with the same speed
The mass is concentrated at one point
The distance between any two particles remains constant
quiz.explain: Rigidity means fixed inter-particle distances.

quiz.q: Which is an example of pure rotation about a fixed axis?
quiz.explain: The fan's axis is fixed; every point moves in a circle.

quiz.q: In pure translational motion of a rigid body
options: All particles have the same velocity at every instant
quiz.explain: Translation means every point moves identically.

quiz.q: In rotation about a fixed axis, a particle of the body moves
options: In a straight line parallel to the axis
In a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis
quiz.explain: Each point traces a circle centred on the axis.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the motion is along the axis

quiz.q: A spinning top whose axis sweeps out a cone about the vertical is an example of
quiz.explain: The tip stays fixed, but the axis itself moves (precession).

quiz.q: The motion of a wheel of a moving bicycle is best described as
options: Pure rotation about a fixed axis
quiz.explain: The hub translates while the wheel rotates about it.
quiz.mistake: Ignores one part of the motion

quiz.q: The body of a car moving along a straight road (ignoring its wheels) is in
quiz.explain: Every point of the car body moves with the same velocity, so it translates.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any vehicle motion involves rotation

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A block sliding down a smooth incline is in pure translation.
Reason (R): All particles of the block have the same velocity at every instant.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Identical velocities for all particles is what pure translation means. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu watches a bicycle and can't decide if its wheel is 'moving' or 'spinning'. Explain rigid bodies and the kinds of motion.
teach.praise: The wheel does both! Its centre translates while it rotates about the hub. Now I see it.
teach.nudge: What is a rigid body? What two kinds of motion can combine for a wheel?

topics.title: Centre of mass of particles and laminas

learn.hook: A gymnast's centre of mass can even lie outside her body during a back-bend. It is a point defined by maths, not by matter.
points: Two particles on a line: X = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂)/(m₁ + m₂). For equal masses it is midway.
n particles in 3D: R = Σmᵢrᵢ/M, i.e. X = Σmᵢxᵢ/M, Y = Σmᵢyᵢ/M, Z = Σmᵢzᵢ/M.
Continuous bodies: X = (1/M)∫x dm etc. For a uniform symmetric body (rod, ring, disc, sphere, cube) the CM lies at the geometric centre.
Uniform triangular lamina: CM at the centroid (intersection of medians).
Composite shapes (e.g. an L-shaped lamina of three equal squares): treat each part as a point mass at its own centre, then combine.

example.q: Masses 1 kg at (0, 0), 1 kg at (4 m, 0) and 2 kg at (0, 4 m). Find the centre of mass.

learn.reallife: Truck loaders in Indian mandis keep heavy sacks low and centred so that the vehicle's centre of mass stays low and it doesn't topple on turns.

items.q: 2 kg at x = 0, 3 kg at x = 5 m: X (m)
1 kg at 0, 1 kg at 6 m: X (m)
3 kg at 0, 1 kg at 8 m: X (m)
Uniform rod from 0 to 2 m: X (m)

games.title: CM facts
items: The centre of mass of two equal masses lies midway between them.
X = (x₁ + x₂)/2.
The centre of mass of a uniform ring lies on the ring.
It is at the centre, where there is no material.
The CM of a uniform triangular lamina is at its centroid.
Where the medians meet.
The CM of two unequal masses is closer to the lighter one.
It is closer to the heavier one.
For a uniform symmetric body, the CM is at its geometric centre.
By symmetry.

quiz.q: A 2 kg mass at x = 0 and a 6 kg mass at x = 4 m. The centre of mass is at x (in m) =
