At any point of the ring
quiz.explain: By symmetry it is at the centre, even though no material is there.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the CM must lie inside material

quiz.q: An L-shaped lamina is made of three identical unit squares placed at (0–1, 0–1), (1–2, 0–1) and (0–1, 1–2) (in m). The x-coordinate of its CM in m is
quiz.mistake: Uses the corners instead of the centres

quiz.q: Masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg are at x = 1 m, 2 m and 3 m. The CM is at x (in m) =
The centre of mass of a uniform triangular lamina lies at
options: The centroid, where the medians meet
The vertex opposite the longest side
quiz.explain: Dividing the lamina into strips parallel to each side puts the CM on every median.

quiz.q: The centre of mass of two particles lies
options: On the line joining them, closer to the heavier one
quiz.explain: m₁d₁ = m₂d₂: the larger mass has the smaller distance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is always the midpoint

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The centre of mass of a body may lie outside the body.
Reason (R): The centre of mass is a mass-weighted average position, not necessarily a material point.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For a ring or a boomerang, the average position is in empty space. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the CM is always inside the material

teach.ask: Gappu thinks the centre of mass of a bangle must be somewhere on the metal. Explain how to find the centre of mass for particles and for symmetric bodies.
teach.praise: It's an average position weighted by mass. For a bangle it's at the centre, in mid-air!
teach.nudge: How do you combine masses and positions? Where would symmetry put the CM of a ring?

topics.title: Motion of the centre of mass

learn.hook: A Diwali rocket bursts into sparks high in the sky. The sparks fly everywhere, but their centre of mass calmly continues on the same parabola.
points: Differentiating MR = Σmᵢrᵢ: MV = Σmᵢvᵢ and MA = Σmᵢaᵢ.
MA = F_ext: the CM moves like a single particle of mass M acted on by the total external force.
Internal forces between particles cancel in third-law pairs, so they cannot affect the motion of the CM.
Exploding projectile: the explosion forces are internal, so the CM keeps following the original parabola (until fragments hit the ground).
The translational motion of a system is the motion of its CM; the rest is motion relative to the CM.

example.q: A shell fired as a projectile explodes into two equal parts at the top of its path. One part falls straight down. Where does the CM land, and where does the other part land?
steps: The CM continues on the original parabola, so it lands at the original range R.
One half lands at R/2 (below the top).
Since the CM is midway between equal halves, the other half lands at 3R/2.
example.answer: CM at R; other piece at 3R/2

learn.reallife: In space-station docking, the internal pushes between astronauts and modules never change the motion of the station's overall centre of mass.

games.title: Showing MA = F_ext
items: Start with MR = Σmᵢrᵢ
Differentiate twice: MA = Σmᵢaᵢ
Each mᵢaᵢ equals the force on particle i
Internal forces cancel in pairs
So MA = F_ext

They cancel in pairs.
After a shell explodes in mid-air, its CM continues on the original path.
Explosion forces are internal.
The CM of a system moves as if all mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted there.
MA = F_ext.
If no external force acts, the CM must be at rest.
It moves with constant velocity (which may be zero).
The CM of a diver doing somersaults follows a parabola.
Only gravity acts externally (ignoring air).

quiz.q: A shell explodes in mid-air into many fragments. Just after the explosion, the centre of mass
options: Moves in a straight horizontal line
Continues on the original parabolic path
quiz.explain: Explosion forces are internal; gravity alone acts on the CM.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the explosion changes the CM's motion

quiz.q: A projectile has range 100 m. At its highest point it splits into two equal parts; one falls vertically. The other lands at (in m from the launch point)
quiz.explain: The CM lands at 100 m; one half at 50 m, so the other at 150 m.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the other piece also lands at 100 m

quiz.explain: MA = F_ext.

quiz.q: Two skaters on frictionless ice pull each other with a rope. Their CM
options: Stays where it was (if initially at rest)
quiz.explain: The rope forces are internal; with no external horizontal force the CM stays at rest.

quiz.q: Masses 2 kg and 3 kg have velocities 5 m s⁻¹ and 0. The velocity of their CM in m s⁻¹ is

quiz.explain: A = F_ext/M = 30/10 = 3 m s⁻².
quiz.mistake: Uses one force or one mass

quiz.q: The translational motion of a system of particles is described by
options: The motion of its centre of mass
The motion of its heaviest particle
The motion of its fastest particle
quiz.explain: The CM carries the 'overall' translation of the system.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When a man walks on a boat floating on still water, the boat moves backward.
Reason (R): With no external horizontal force, the CM of the man–boat system does not move.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: To keep the CM fixed, the boat must move opposite to the man. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the boat moves because of water currents

teach.ask: Gappu saw a firecracker explode in the sky and thinks its 'middle' changed path. Explain the motion of the centre of mass.
teach.praise: The sparks scatter, but their CM keeps flying on the original parabola. Internal forces can't change it!
teach.nudge: Which forces can change the motion of the CM? What does the CM do after the explosion?

topics.title: Linear momentum of a system and its conservation

learn.hook: Two stars orbit each other in a binary system. They whirl around wildly, yet their centre of mass glides through space in a straight line.
points: Total momentum P = Σmᵢvᵢ = MV.
dP/dt = F_ext: only external forces change the total momentum.
If F_ext = 0, P is constant, so the CM moves with constant velocity (or stays at rest).
Radioactive decay of a nucleus at rest: the products fly apart in opposite directions so that the CM stays at rest.
Binary stars: under their mutual gravity (internal), the CM moves uniformly while the stars orbit around it.

example.q: A uranium-238 nucleus at rest decays into a thorium nucleus (234 u) and an alpha particle (4 u) moving at 1.17 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Find the thorium speed.
steps: Initial P = 0, so the products' momenta are equal and opposite.
v = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, opposite to the alpha particle.

learn.reallife: Astronomers at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics use the wobble of a star about the common CM to detect unseen companion planets.

games.title: Momentum of a system
items: P = MV, where V is the CM velocity.
Sum of mᵢvᵢ equals MV.
Internal forces can change total momentum.
dP/dt = F_ext.
If a nucleus at rest decays into two parts, they move in opposite directions.
Total momentum stays zero.
In a binary star system the CM moves in an ellipse.
With no external force it moves uniformly.
The lighter decay product moves faster.
Equal momenta: speed ∝ 1/m.

quiz.q: A nucleus at rest splits into two fragments of masses in the ratio 1 : 3. The ratio of their speeds (lighter : heavier) is
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite momenta: m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ → v₁/v₂ = m₂/m₁ = 3.

quiz.q: For a system with no external force, which must be constant?
options: Velocity of the centre of mass
quiz.explain: dP/dt = 0 → MV constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every particle's motion is fixed

quiz.q: Total momentum of a system equals
options: Mass of the heaviest particle × its velocity
Total mass × velocity of the CM
quiz.explain: P = MV.

quiz.q: A 200 u nucleus at rest emits a 4 u particle at 2 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. The recoil speed of the remaining 196 u nucleus, in units of 10⁵ m s⁻¹, is about
Two stars of a binary system attract each other gravitationally. With no other forces, their CM
quiz.explain: Mutual gravity is internal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gravity between the stars moves the CM

quiz.q: dP/dt for a system of particles equals
quiz.explain: Internal forces sum to zero.

quiz.q: A 3 kg body at 4 m s⁻¹ and a 1 kg body at −4 m s⁻¹ (along x). The total momentum in kg m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: P = 12 − 4 = 8 kg m s⁻¹.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The products of a decay of a nucleus at rest fly off in opposite directions.
Reason (R): The total linear momentum of the isolated system must remain zero.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Zero initial momentum must stay zero, which requires opposite momenta. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they can fly the same way

teach.ask: Gappu watched two stars spinning around each other in a planetarium show and asks what stays steady. Explain total momentum and the CM.
teach.praise: The stars dance, but their CM cruises at constant velocity because no outside force acts!
teach.nudge: What is the total momentum of a system in terms of its CM? When is it conserved?

topics.title: The vector (cross) product

learn.hook: Tighten a screw clockwise and it goes in. That everyday rule is exactly how the direction of a cross product is decided.
points: a × b = ab sin θ n̂, where n̂ is perpendicular to both a and b. Direction by the right-hand rule (fingers from a to b, thumb gives a × b) or a right-handed screw.
Properties: anticommutative (a × b = −b × a), distributive, and a × a = 0.
Unit vectors: î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ; reversing the order gives a minus sign; î × î = 0.
Component (determinant) form: a × b = (a_yb_z − a_zb_y)î + (a_zbₓ − aₓb_z)ĵ + (aₓb_y − a_ybₓ)k̂.
Under reflection, ordinary (polar) vectors change sign but a × b does not: the cross product is an axial (pseudo) vector.

example.q: Find a·b and a × b for a = î + 2ĵ and b = 3î + ĵ.

learn.reallife: Mechanics at a two-wheeler service centre know 'righty-tighty, lefty-loosey' without thinking: it's the right-handed screw rule.

games.title: Cross-product facts
items: a × b = b × a.
It is anticommutative: a × b = −b × a.
a × b is perpendicular to both a and b.
It is along n̂.
The magnitude of a × b is ab sin θ.
It equals the area of the parallelogram formed by a and b.
a × a = a².
The cross product does not change sign under reflection.
It is an axial vector.

quiz.q: The cross product î × k̂ equals
quiz.explain: k̂ × î = ĵ, so î × k̂ = −ĵ.

quiz.explain: sin θ = 0 means θ = 0° or 180°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the dot product condition

For a = î + ĵ and b = ĵ + k̂, a × b equals
quiz.mistake: Misses the minus sign on the ĵ term

quiz.q: The cross product is
quiz.explain: a × b = −b × a and a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.

quiz.q: The magnitude of a × b equals
options: The area of the parallelogram with sides a and b
quiz.explain: ab sin θ is base × height of the parallelogram.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The vector product of a vector with itself is the null vector.
Reason (R): The angle between a vector and itself is zero and sin 0° = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: |a × a| = a² sin 0° = 0. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a × b and b × a are the same, just like 2 × 3 and 3 × 2. Explain the cross product, its direction and its properties.
teach.praise: So a × b points one way and b × a points the opposite way! Right-hand rule for the win.
teach.nudge: What is the size of a × b? Which way does it point, and what happens if you swap the order?

topics.title: Angular velocity and angular acceleration

learn.hook: Every point on a spinning CD turns through the same angle each second, but the outer rim races far faster than the inside.
points: Angular velocity ω is a vector along the axis of rotation; its direction follows the right-hand rule (curl fingers with the rotation, thumb gives ω).
Linear velocity of a particle: v = ω × r; magnitude v = ωr⊥, where r⊥ is the perpendicular distance from the axis.
All particles of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis share the same ω; only v differs (∝ distance from axis). Points on the axis have v = 0.
Angular acceleration α = dω/dt. For rotation about a fixed axis, both ω and α lie along the axis.

example.q: A disc rotates at ω = 10 rad s⁻¹. Find the speed of points 0.05 m and 0.15 m from the axis.

learn.reallife: The Earth's angular velocity is the same everywhere (about 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹), but a person in Chennai moves faster than one in Srinagar because Chennai is farther from the axis.

items.q: ω from 2 to 8 rad/s in 3 s: α (rad/s²)
Double the distance from axis: v becomes × ?

games.title: Angular velocity facts
items: All particles of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis have the same angular velocity.
They turn through the same angle in the same time.
Points farther from the axis have larger angular velocity.
Same ω, larger linear speed.
Angular velocity is a vector along the axis of rotation.
Direction by the right-hand rule.
v = ω × r gives a velocity along the axis.
It is perpendicular to both ω and r.
For fixed-axis rotation, angular acceleration is along the axis.
ω changes only in magnitude.

quiz.q: A wheel rotates at 20 rad s⁻¹. The linear speed of a point 0.3 m from the axis in m s⁻¹ is
The direction of the angular velocity of a wheel rotating anticlockwise (as seen from above) is
quiz.explain: Right-hand rule: curl fingers anticlockwise, thumb points up.
quiz.mistake: Uses the left hand or thinks ω is tangential

quiz.q: Two points A and B on a rotating disc are at distances 2 cm and 6 cm from the axis. The ratio v_A : v_B is
quiz.explain: Same ω, so v ∝ r: 2/6 = 1/3.

quiz.q: The angular velocity of a fan increases from 10 rad s⁻¹ to 30 rad s⁻¹ in 4 s. Its average angular acceleration in rad s⁻² is
quiz.explain: α = Δω/Δt = 20/4 = 5 rad s⁻².

quiz.q: Which quantity is the same for all particles of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis?
quiz.explain: Every particle turns through the same angle in the same time.

quiz.explain: k̂ × î = ĵ, so v = 6ĵ m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: The Earth rotates once in 24 h (86400 s). Its angular speed in units of 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹ is about
quiz.mistake: Uses hours or minutes instead of seconds

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Points on the rim of a rotating wheel move faster than points near the hub.
Reason (R): Points on the rim have a larger angular velocity than points near the hub.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: all points of a rigid wheel share the same ω; the rim is faster because v = ωr⊥.

teach.ask: Gappu sits near the centre of a merry-go-round and his friend on the edge. Gappu thinks his friend 'rotates faster'. Explain angular velocity versus linear speed.
teach.praise: We both turn at the same ω; my friend just moves faster because he's farther out. v = ωr!
teach.nudge: Do you both turn through the same angle each second? Then why is your friend's speed larger?

topics.title: Torque and angular momentum of a particle

learn.hook: Ever tried opening a door by pushing near its hinge? Same force, almost no turning. Torque depends on where you push.
points: Torque (moment of force): τ = r × F, magnitude τ = rF sin θ. SI unit N m (not written as joule). It is a vector along the axis by the right-hand rule.
τ = F × r⊥ (moment arm: perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of F) = r × F⊥.
Angular momentum of a particle: l = r × p, magnitude l = rp sin θ = r⊥ p.
Rotational analogue of F = dp/dt: dl/dt = τ.

example.q: A force F = 3î N acts at r = î + 2ĵ m. Find the torque about the origin.
steps: τ = −6k̂ N m (clockwise as seen from +z).

learn.reallife: Spanners for truck wheel nuts in highway dhabas are long, so mechanics get a big moment arm and loosen tight nuts with modest force.

quiz.explain: τ = F × r⊥: bigger r⊥, bigger torque.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is only for convenience

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Torque and work have different dimensions.
Reason (R): Torque is a vector quantity while work is a scalar.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: both have dimensions [M L² T⁻²]. R is true, but being a vector does not change dimensions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks vectors and scalars cannot share dimensions

teach.ask: Gappu pushes a door right next to its hinge and it barely moves. Explain torque, moment arm and angular momentum.
teach.praise: Push far from the hinge to get a big moment arm and a big torque! And torque changes angular momentum.
teach.nudge: What two things decide the torque? What does torque change?

topics.title: Systems: dL/dt = τ_ext and conservation of angular momentum

learn.hook: Planets sweep around the Sun for billions of years without slowing down because there is no external torque on them about the Sun.
points: For a system of particles, L = Σlᵢ and dL/dt = τ_ext. Internal torques cancel in pairs (internal forces are equal, opposite and along the same line).
Conservation: if τ_ext = 0, the total angular momentum L is constant (in magnitude and direction).
A particle moving with constant velocity has constant angular momentum about any point: l = r⊥ mv with r⊥ (distance of the line from the point) fixed.
Central forces (gravity of the Sun) produce no torque about the centre, so planets' angular momentum is conserved.

example.q: Show that a 1 kg particle moving at 2 m s⁻¹ along the line y = 3 m has constant angular momentum about the origin.
steps: x has dropped out, so l = −6k̂ kg m² s⁻¹ at all times.

learn.reallife: ISRO's satellites use spinning momentum wheels: changing a wheel's spin makes the satellite turn the other way, keeping total angular momentum fixed.

Not zero unless the line passes through the point; but it is constant.
If τ_ext = 0, L is conserved.
dL/dt = 0.
Gravity of the Sun exerts no torque on a planet about the Sun.
The force passes through the Sun.
dL/dt = τ_ext is the rotational analogue of dP/dt = F_ext.
Same structure.

topics.title: Equilibrium of a rigid body, couples and levers

learn.hook: Turning a car's steering wheel with both hands applies a couple: it spins the wheel without pushing it anywhere.
points: Mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body: net external force = 0 (translational) AND net external torque = 0 (rotational).
In 3D these give six independent conditions: three force components and three torque components equal to zero.
A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces with different lines of action. It produces rotation without translation; its torque = F × d (d = separation), the same about any point.
Principle of moments (lever): load × load arm = effort × effort arm. Mechanical advantage MA = load/effort = effort arm/load arm.

example.q: A see-saw is balanced at its centre. A 30 kg child sits 2 m from the pivot. Where must a 40 kg child sit to balance it?
steps: Principle of moments about the pivot: 30g × 2 = 40g × d.
Sit 1.5 m from the pivot on the other side.

learn.reallife: A hand-pump in an Indian village is a lever: a long handle (effort arm) lets a small push lift a heavy column of water.

teach.nudge: Is zero net force enough for balance? What must also be zero? How do you balance a see-saw?

topics.title: Centre of gravity and equilibrium problems

learn.hook: Tall structures, from the Qutub Minar to modern Mumbai skyscrapers, stand safely because their centre of gravity lies low and well within a wide base.
points: Centre of gravity (CG): the point where the total gravitational torque on the body is zero. In a uniform g, the CG coincides with the CM.
Finding CG of an irregular lamina: suspend it from a point and draw the vertical (plumb line); repeat from another point. The CG is where the lines cross.
Bar on two supports: use ΣF = 0 for the sum of reactions and Στ = 0 about one support for each reaction.
Ladder against a smooth wall: the wall gives only a horizontal push; the floor gives a vertical normal force and friction. Take torques about the foot.
Car on its wheels: take moments about one axle to split the weight between front and rear wheels.

example.q: A uniform 1 m bar of 2 kg rests on supports at its ends A and B. A 4 kg load hangs 0.25 m from A (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the reactions.
steps: Weights: bar 20 N at 0.5 m, load 40 N at 0.25 m.

learn.reallife: Truck designers place the engine and load so the weight is shared safely between the front and rear axles. Lab safety: when locating a lamina's CG by suspension, push the pin through a pre-made hole and keep fingers away from its sharp point.

Mark the second vertical
The CG is where the two lines intersect

A freely suspended body comes to rest with its CG vertically below the point of suspension.
Then gravity's torque is zero.
A smooth wall exerts a vertical force on a ladder.
Smooth means only a normal, horizontal push.
The CG of a very tall building is exactly at its CM even though g varies slightly with height.
Strictly, they differ slightly when g is not uniform.

topics.title: Moment of inertia and radius of gyration

learn.hook: A tightrope walker carries a long pole. Spreading mass far from the axis makes her much harder to topple: that's moment of inertia.
points: Rotational KE: K = ½Iω², with moment of inertia I = Σmᵢrᵢ² (rᵢ = distance from the axis). Unit kg m².
I depends on the mass, its distribution, and the axis chosen. It is the rotational analogue of mass (measure of rotational inertia).
Thin ring about its axis (through centre, ⊥ plane): MR². Thin rod about a ⊥ axis through its centre: ML²/12.
Standard values: disc or solid cylinder about its axis MR²/2; hollow cylinder about its axis MR²; ring about a diameter MR²/2; disc about a diameter MR²/4; solid sphere about a diameter (2/5)MR².
Radius of gyration k: I = Mk², so k = √(I/M). For a ring about its axis k = R; for a disc about its axis k = R/√2.

example.q: A ring of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m spins at 10 rad s⁻¹ about its axis. Find I and the rotational KE.

learn.reallife: Kabaddi and wrestling coaches teach athletes to tuck limbs in to turn quickly: a smaller I means less effort to start rotation.

topics.title: Flywheels and kinematics of rotation

learn.hook: Old bullock-driven sugarcane crushers and modern car engines both use heavy flywheels so the rotation doesn't jerk.
points: A flywheel has a large moment of inertia, so it resists changes in angular speed and smooths out the jerky torque of an engine.
Analogues: θ ↔ x, ω ↔ v, α ↔ a.
For constant α: ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2α(θ − θ₀).
Revolutions = θ/(2π); rpm to rad s⁻¹: multiply by 2π/60.

example.q: A wheel starts from rest with α = 2 rad s⁻². Find ω and θ after 5 s, and the number of revolutions.

learn.reallife: The flywheel on a single-cylinder motorbike engine keeps the single cylinder's power pulses from shaking the bike.

quiz.q: A motor wheel's angular speed rises from 20 rad s⁻¹ to 40 rad s⁻¹ in 10 s. Its angular acceleration in rad s⁻² is

quiz.explain: θ = ω₀t + ½αt² = 200 + 100 = 300 rad (or average ω 30 × 10).

quiz.q: A fan at 30 rad s⁻¹ is switched off and stops in 10 s with uniform deceleration. The angle turned while stopping in rad is
A wheel starts from rest and turns through 100 rad in 10 s with constant α. Its α in rad s⁻² is
The main purpose of a flywheel in an engine is to
options: Keep the angular speed steady because of its large moment of inertia
quiz.explain: Large I resists changes in ω, smoothing out uneven torque.

quiz.q: A disc speeds up from rest to 6 rad s⁻¹ with α = 3 rad s⁻². The angle turned in rad is
quiz.explain: ω² = 2αθ → θ = 36/6 = 6 rad.

quiz.explain: 120 rev/min = 2 rev/s = 2 × 2π = 4π ≈ 12.56 rad s⁻¹.

quiz.q:

Reason (R): Angular acceleration is measured in rad s⁻².
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the unit of α does not explain why the equation needs constant α.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true but irrelevant fact

teach.ask: Gappu's grandfather's sugarcane crusher has a heavy wheel and Gappu wants to calculate how many turns it makes when speeding up. Explain flywheels and rotational kinematics.
teach.praise: Just swap x, v, a for θ, ω, α and use the same three equations. Then divide by 2π for turns!
teach.nudge: What does the heavy wheel do for the machine? Which equations describe constant angular acceleration?

topics.title: Dynamics of rotation: τ = Iα, work and power

learn.hook: Pull the rope of a well's pulley and the drum spins up. τ = Iα tells you exactly how fast.
points: For rotation about a fixed axis, only torque components along the axis matter; perpendicular components are balanced by the bearings.
Work done by a torque: dW = τ dθ, so W = τθ for constant τ. Power P = τω.
Second law for rotation: τ = Iα.
Analogues: m ↔ I, F ↔ τ, p = mv ↔ L = Iω, K = ½mv² ↔ ½Iω², W = Fx ↔ τθ, P = Fv ↔ τω.
Cord wound on a flywheel and pulled with F: τ = FR, α = FR/I; work done = F × length pulled = gain in ½Iω².

example.q: A cord on the rim of a 10 kg disc flywheel (R = 0.2 m) is pulled with 20 N. Find α, and ω after 2 m of cord is pulled (from rest).
steps: τ = FR = 4 N m; α = τ/I = 20 rad s⁻².
example.answer: α = 20 rad s⁻², ω = 20 rad s⁻¹

learn.reallife: Ceiling-fan makers in India rate motors by power: P = τω tells how much torque the motor supplies at its running speed.

topics.title: Angular momentum about a fixed axis and its conservation

learn.hook: A Bharatanatyam dancer spinning on one foot pulls her arms in and suddenly whirls faster. No push, just angular momentum conservation.
points: For rotation about a fixed axis: L = Iω, and dL/dt = τ (axial component).
If the external torque is zero, Iω = constant: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.
Examples: a person on a rotating stool pulling in arms (I decreases, ω increases); a diver tucking in to somersault faster; a skater spinning.
Rotational KE changes: K = L²/(2I). With L fixed, reducing I increases K; the extra energy comes from the work done by the person's muscles.
Typical numericals: torque on a disc from τ = Iα, L = Iω, and K = ½Iω².

example.q: A child on a turntable has I = 6 kg m² with arms out, spinning at 2 rad s⁻¹. Folding arms makes I = 2 kg m². Find the new ω and the ratio of KE.
steps: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ → 6 × 2 = 2 × ω₂ → ω₂ = 6 rad s⁻¹.
KE triples; the child's muscles supply the extra 24 J.

learn.reallife: Divers at national aquatics championships tuck tightly to complete multiple somersaults, then open out to slow the spin before entering the water.

topics.title: From geocentric skies to Kepler's law of orbits

learn.hook: The same force that makes a mango drop from a tree in Malihabad keeps the Moon circling the Earth. It took humanity two thousand years to see that.
points: Everything near the Earth tends to fall towards it. The motion of planets puzzled thinkers for centuries: Ptolemy's geocentric model put the Earth at the centre.
Aryabhata (5th century CE) described the Earth rotating on its axis; Copernicus (16th century) proposed the heliocentric model with the Sun at the centre.

Tycho Brahe made precise naked-eye records of planetary positions; Kepler analysed them to find three laws; Galileo showed all bodies fall with the same acceleration; Newton explained it all with universal gravitation.
Kepler's first law (law of orbits): every planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
Perihelion: the point of closest approach to the Sun; aphelion: the farthest point.

example.q: A planet's orbit has perihelion distance 1.0 AU and aphelion distance 1.5 AU. Find the semi-major axis.
steps: The major axis = perihelion + aphelion distance = 2.5 AU.

learn.reallife: Jantar Mantar observatories built in Jaipur and Delhi were used to track the Sun, Moon and planets with remarkable precision long before telescopes were common in India.

topics.title: Kepler's laws of areas and periods

learn.hook: The Earth moves fastest in early January, when it is closest to the Sun. Kepler's second law predicted this centuries ago.
points: Second law (law of areas): the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.
Reason: gravity is a central force, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and the planet's angular momentum L is conserved. Areal velocity dA/dt = L/(2m) = constant.
Hence a planet moves faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion: v_p r_p = v_a r_a.
Third law (law of periods): T² ∝ a³, where a is the semi-major axis. T²/a³ is nearly the same for all planets of the Sun.

example.q: A comet's speed at perihelion (r = 1 AU) is 60 km s⁻¹. Find its speed at aphelion (r = 5 AU).
steps: Angular momentum is conserved: v_p r_p = v_a r_a.

learn.reallife: ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission moved in a highly elliptical orbit around Mars, speeding up near periapsis exactly as the law of areas predicts.

topics.title: Newton's universal law of gravitation

learn.hook: You and the person next to you attract each other gravitationally right now. The force is about a millionth of a newton, far too tiny to feel.
points: Every particle attracts every other particle with F = Gm₁m₂/r², along the line joining them.
Vector form: the force on m₂ due to m₁ is F₂₁ = −(Gm₁m₂/r²) r̂₁₂, where r̂₁₂ points from m₁ to m₂; the minus sign shows attraction.
Gravitational force is always attractive, central (along the line of centres) and obeys superposition: the net force is the vector sum of forces from each mass.
Three equal masses at the vertices of an equilateral triangle exert zero net force on a mass at the centroid (by symmetry).

example.q: Find the gravitational force between two 100 kg spheres whose centres are 1 m apart (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
steps: Tiny compared with their weights (about 980 N each).

learn.reallife: The tides at the Gulf of Khambhat, among the highest in India, are driven by the Moon's and Sun's gravitational pull on the oceans.

topics.title: Shell theorem, Newton's Moon test and measuring G

learn.hook: Newton asked: if gravity reaches the apple, does it reach the Moon? He checked using nothing more than the Moon's orbit and the inverse-square law.
points: Shell theorem: a uniform spherical shell attracts an outside point mass as if all its mass were at its centre. Inside the shell, the net force is zero.
Moon test: the Moon is about 60 Earth radii away. Its centripetal acceleration a_m = 4π²R_m/T² ≈ 0.0027 m s⁻², and g/a_m ≈ 3600 = 60², just as the inverse-square law predicts.
Cavendish (1798) measured G with a torsion balance: two small lead spheres on a rod hung from a fine wire, attracted by two large spheres; the twist of the wire gave the force.
Accepted value: G ≈ 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

example.q: Show that the Moon's acceleration agrees with the inverse-square law if the Moon is 60 Earth radii away.
steps: At the surface (r = R), acceleration = g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻².
At r = 60R, acceleration should be g/60² = 9.8/3600.
= 0.0027 m s⁻², matching 4π²R_m/T² for the Moon.

learn.reallife: Precise measurements of G are still being improved worldwide, because G is the least precisely known of the fundamental constants.

topics.title: Acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface

learn.hook: Knowing just g, the Earth's radius and G, you can 'weigh' the entire Earth from your physics lab.
points: Treat the Earth as concentric uniform shells: for any outside point, the Earth acts as a point mass M_E at its centre.
At the surface: mg = GM_E m/R_E², so g = GM_E/R_E².
Mass of the Earth: M_E = gR_E²/G = 9.8 × (6.37 × 10⁶)²/(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹) ≈ 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.
Weight W = mg. g does not depend on the mass of the falling body, so (without air) all bodies fall with the same acceleration.

example.q: A planet has twice the Earth's mass and twice its radius. Compare g on it with g on the Earth.
steps: So g on the planet is g/2.

topics.title: Variation of g with height and depth

learn.hook: Climbers on Mount Everest weigh about 0.3% less than at sea level, and in a deep mine g also drops. The surface is where g peaks.
points: Height h: g(h) = GM/(R + h)² = g(1 + h/R)⁻² ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) for h ≪ R.
Depth d: only the inner sphere of radius (R − d) attracts (the outer shell gives zero), so g(d) = g(1 − d/R).
g is maximum at the surface, decreases with height and with depth, and is zero at the centre.
At h = R, g becomes g/4; at d = R/2, g becomes g/2. Small heights: g falls by about twice as fast with height as with depth.

topics.title: Gravitational potential energy

learn.hook: Lifting a satellite to orbit costs energy. How much? You can't use mgh for thousands of kilometres; you need the general formula.
points: Gravitational force is conservative, so we can define potential energy: the work done by gravity depends only on start and end positions.
Near the surface (h ≪ R): the PE difference between heights h₁ and h₂ is mg(h₂ − h₁).
General expression, taking PE = 0 at infinity: W(r) = −GM_E m/r for r ≥ R_E. It is negative and increases (towards zero) as r increases.
Work needed to move m from r₁ to r₂ = W(r₂) − W(r₁) = GM_E m(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).

example.q: Find the work needed to raise a 1 kg mass from the Earth's surface to a height R (in terms of GM/R).
steps: = GMm/2R = ½ gR m (using GM = gR²).

learn.reallife: PSLV launches to sun-synchronous orbits at about 700 km lift satellites high enough that mgh is no longer accurate: engineers use −GMm/r.

topics.title: Gravitational potential and systems of particles

learn.hook: The total gravitational energy of a star cluster is the sum of the energy of every pair. Four particles? That's six pairs.
points: Gravitational potential V at a point = PE per unit mass: V = −GM/r (unit J kg⁻¹). It is a scalar.
Potentials from several masses add as scalars: V = −G Σ mᵢ/rᵢ.
PE of a system of particles = sum over all pairs: U = −G Σ mᵢmⱼ/rᵢⱼ (each pair counted once).
Four equal masses m at the corners of a square of side l: 4 sides and 2 diagonals (l√2), so U = −(Gm²/l)(4 + √2). Potential at the centre (distance l/√2 from each) = −4√2 Gm/l.

example.q: Three equal masses m are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side a. Find the PE of the system.
steps: Number of pairs = 3, each separated by a.

topics.title: Escape speed

learn.hook: Throw a ball up at 11.2 km s⁻¹ (ignoring air) and it never comes back. That's the Earth's escape speed.
points: A body escapes if its total energy is ≥ 0: ½mv² − GMm/R ≥ 0.
Minimum (escape) speed: v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR). For the Earth (g = 9.8 m s⁻², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m) v_e ≈ 11.2 km s⁻¹.
Escape speed does not depend on the mass of the body or the direction of launch (ignoring air).
The Moon's escape speed is only about 2.3 km s⁻¹. It is so low that the faster gas molecules escape over time, so the Moon has no atmosphere.
Between two fixed spheres: a projectile must reach the 'neutral point' where the two pulls balance; beyond it, the far sphere pulls it in.

example.q: Calculate the Earth's escape speed with g = 9.8 m s⁻² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.

learn.reallife: Chandrayaan missions do not leave Earth at 11.2 km s⁻¹ directly; they raise their orbit step by step with engine burns, gaining energy gradually.

topics.title: Earth satellites: orbital speed and period

learn.hook: A satellite skimming just above the Earth would circle the planet in about 85 minutes, faster than a cricket Test session!
points: Satellites are natural (the Moon) or artificial (INSAT, Cartosat). In a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: mv²/(R + h) = GMm/(R + h)².
Orbital speed v = √(GM/(R + h)); it decreases with height. Near the surface v ≈ √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km s⁻¹.
Period T = 2π√((R + h)³/GM), so T² ∝ (R + h)³: Kepler's third law for satellites.
For h ≪ R: T ≈ 2π√(R/g) ≈ 85 minutes.
From a moon's orbit we can find the planet's mass: M = 4π²r³/(GT²) (e.g. Mars from its moon Phobos; Earth from the Moon).

example.q: Find the period of a satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

learn.reallife: ISRO's geostationary communication satellites like GSAT orbit at about 36000 km height with a 24-hour period, staying fixed over India.

topics.title: Energy of an orbiting satellite

learn.hook: To move a satellite to a higher orbit, you must ADD energy, even though it will end up moving more slowly. Strange but true.
points: Kinetic energy in a circular orbit of radius r = R + h: K = GMm/(2r).
Potential energy: U = −GMm/r.
Total energy E = K + U = −GMm/(2r). It is negative for a bound orbit, and K = −E, U = 2E.
Energy to move from orbit r₁ to r₂: ΔE = (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) > 0 for r₂ > r₁.
Conceptual points: gravity cannot be shielded by any material; weight changes with height and depth; g is slightly smaller at the equator than at the poles (Earth's rotation and bulge).

example.q: A satellite in an orbit of radius 2R has total energy E. What is its energy in an orbit of radius 4R, and how much energy is needed to shift it?

learn.reallife: Satellite operators at ISRO's ISTRAC in Bengaluru fire thrusters to raise orbits that slowly decay because of thin atmospheric drag.

topics.title: Elasticity and plasticity

learn.hook: Stretch a rubber band and it snaps back; squeeze a lump of atta dough and it stays squashed. Same push, very different materials.
points: A rigid body is only an idealisation: every real body deforms (changes shape or size) when forces act on it.
Elasticity: the property of a body to regain its original size and shape when the deforming force is removed.
Plasticity: the body does not regain its shape and is permanently deformed.
Elastic examples: steel, rubber (within limits); nearly plastic examples: putty, wet clay, mud, dough.
Engineers must know elastic behaviour to design bridges, buildings, cranes, machines and even artificial body parts.

example.q: A steel spring is stretched slightly and released; a clay ball is pressed and released. Classify each behaviour.
steps: The spring returns to its original length: elastic.
The clay keeps its new dented shape: plastic.
So steel (within limits) is elastic and clay is plastic.

learn.reallife: The pottery artisans of Khurja rely on the plasticity of wet clay to shape cups and vases on the wheel.

topics.title: Stress: longitudinal, shearing and hydraulic

learn.hook: A heavy train crossing the Chenab rail bridge sets up stresses inside every steel member. Engineers calculate each one.
points: When a body is deformed, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area = F/A. SI unit N m⁻² = pascal (Pa).
Longitudinal stress: force normal to the cross-section. Tensile stress when stretched, compressive stress when compressed.
Shearing (tangential) stress: force parallel to the surface (e.g. pushing the top of a book sideways).
Hydraulic (volume) stress: equal force per unit area on all sides (e.g. a body deep in water); it equals the pressure.

topics.title: Strain and Hooke's law

learn.hook: Hang a 1 kg mass on a 1 m steel wire and it stretches less than a hair's width. Strain measures that tiny change as a fraction.
points: Strain = fractional change in size or shape. Longitudinal strain = ΔL/L; shearing strain = Δx/L = tan θ ≈ θ; volume strain = ΔV/V.
Strain is a ratio of like quantities, so it has no units or dimensions.
Hooke's law: for small deformations, stress ∝ strain, i.e. stress = k × strain.
The proportionality constant k is the modulus of elasticity (Young's, shear or bulk modulus, depending on the type of stress).
Hooke's law is an empirical law and holds only within the elastic (proportional) limit.

topics.title: The stress–strain curve

learn.hook: Testing labs pull a steel rod until it snaps, plotting stress against strain. That curve tells engineers everything about the metal.
points: For a metal under tension, the curve starts as a straight line (O to A): Hooke's law holds up to the proportional limit.
Beyond A, up to the yield point (elastic limit) B, the body still returns to its shape but stress is no longer proportional to strain. The stress at B is the yield strength σ_y.
Beyond B is the plastic region: if the load is removed (say at C), the body does not return; the remaining strain is the permanent set.
Stress rises to a maximum, the ultimate tensile strength σ_u (point D); beyond it, the wire thins locally and breaks at the fracture point E, even with less stress.

example.q: On a stress–strain curve, a wire is loaded to point C beyond the yield point and unloaded. What happens?
steps: C lies in the plastic region.
When unloaded, the curve comes down roughly parallel to OA but does not reach O.
The wire keeps a permanent strain called the permanent set.

learn.reallife: Steel plants grade TMT bars for Indian construction by their yield strength, e.g. 'Fe 500' means a yield strength of about 500 MPa.

topics.title: Ductile, brittle and elastomeric materials

learn.hook: Copper can be drawn into thin wires; a glass rod just snaps. The stress–strain curve explains why.
points: Ductile materials (copper, aluminium, mild steel) have a large plastic region between the ultimate tensile strength and fracture; they can be drawn into wires.
Brittle materials (glass, cast iron, ceramics) fracture soon after the ultimate tensile strength is reached, with little plastic flow.
Elastomers (rubber, the tissue of the aorta) can be stretched to large strains and still return; their curve has no well-defined linear (Hooke's law) region.
Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber, so for the same stress it strains far less. In the physics sense, steel is MORE elastic than rubber.

example.q: Two wires of the same size, one of steel (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) and one of copper (Y = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa), carry equal loads. Which stretches more?
steps: ΔL = FL/(AY), so ΔL ∝ 1/Y for the same F, L, A.

teach.nudge: What does 'more elastic' mean in physics? Which is ductile, copper or glass?

topics.title: Young's modulus

learn.hook: The steel cables of a lift at a Mumbai high-rise stretch a few millimetres every time people step in. Young's modulus predicts exactly how much.
points: Young's modulus Y = longitudinal stress/longitudinal strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). Unit N m⁻² (Pa).
Elongation: ΔL = FL/(AY). Thicker, shorter, stiffer wires stretch less.
Typical values: steel about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; copper about 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa; aluminium about 7 × 10¹⁰ Pa. (B and G values are also tabulated for materials.)
Two wires joined end to end carrying a load: both have the same tension F. Stress in each = F/A for that wire; elongations add up.

example.q: A 2 m steel wire (A = 10⁻⁶ m², Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) holds a 100 N load. Find the elongation.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' overhead wire for electric locomotives is kept under carefully calculated tension, using Young's modulus to control sag and stretch.

teach.nudge: What is Young's modulus? Which factors make a wire stretch more?

topics.title: Shear modulus and bulk modulus

learn.hook: At the deepest point of the Indian Ocean, water is under over 700 atmospheres of pressure, yet its volume shrinks by only about 3%.
points: Shear (rigidity) modulus G = shearing stress/shearing strain = (F/A)/(Δx/L) = FL/(AΔx). For most materials G ≈ Y/3.
Shear displacement of a slab: Δx = FL/(AG).
Bulk modulus B = −p/(ΔV/V) (the minus sign makes B positive, since volume decreases when pressure increases). Compressibility k = 1/B.
Solids have the largest B, liquids smaller, gases the smallest: gases are the most compressible.
Water has B ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa; glass about 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

example.q: Water (B = 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa) is subjected to an extra pressure of 2.2 × 10⁷ Pa. Find the fractional decrease in volume.

learn.reallife: Submarines of the Indian Navy are built to withstand enormous hydraulic stress; their hulls use materials with high bulk modulus.

teach.praise: Shear changes shape, bulk changes volume. Gases have tiny B, so they squash the easiest!
teach.nudge: What does shear modulus measure? What does bulk modulus measure? Which state is easiest to compress?

topics.title: Poisson's ratio and elastic energy

learn.hook: Stretch a rubber band and watch it get thinner. That sideways shrinking, compared with the stretch, is Poisson's ratio.
points: When a wire is stretched, it also gets thinner. Lateral strain = Δd/d; longitudinal strain = ΔL/L.
Poisson's ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain (magnitudes). It has no units or dimensions; for steel it is about 0.28–0.30.
Work done in stretching a wire is stored as elastic potential energy: U = ½ × stress × strain × volume = ½ F ΔL.
Energy density (per unit volume): u = ½ × stress × strain = ½ Y (strain)² = (stress)²/(2Y).

example.q: A wire stretched by 2 mm under a final load of 100 N. Find the elastic energy stored.

learn.reallife: Catapult (gulel) users in villages store elastic energy in stretched rubber; the energy is ½ × stress × strain × volume of the rubber.

teach.ask: Gappu stretched a rubber vine to launch a seed and noticed it got thinner. Explain Poisson's ratio and the energy stored in a stretched wire.
teach.praise: Thinner as it gets longer: Poisson's ratio! And the energy stored is ½ × stress × strain × volume.
teach.nudge: How do you compare the thinning with the stretching? How much energy does a stretched wire store?

topics.title: Applications of elastic behaviour

learn.hook: Why are bridge girders shaped like the letter I, and why can't mountains on Earth be much taller than about 10 km? Elasticity answers both.
points: Crane ropes: the rope's area must keep stress below the yield strength, with a safety factor (say 10). Ropes are made of many thin wires twisted together for flexibility and strength.

Beams: sag of a beam (length l, breadth b, depth d) loaded at the middle: δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y). Increasing depth d reduces sag greatly (d³), so beams are deep; an I-section saves material and resists buckling.
Pillars with distributed (bevelled) ends carry more load than those with rounded ends.
Mountains: the rock at the base would flow under shear stress if a mountain were much taller than about 10 km on Earth.
Typical numericals: elongations with Y, shear displacements with G, volume changes with B, and ratios of elongations for different wires.

example.q: A crane must lift 10⁴ kg. The rope's yield strength is 3 × 10⁸ Pa (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the minimum cross-sectional area, and with a safety factor of 10.
steps: With safety factor 10: A ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻³ m² (radius about 3 cm).

learn.reallife: The I-shaped steel girders used in Delhi Metro's elevated viaducts are chosen to resist bending with minimum steel.

teach.nudge: Which dimension of a beam reduces sag the most? How do engineers make sure a rope won't fail?

topics.title: Fluids, pressure and density

learn.hook: A sharp needle pierces your skin with a gentle push, while a wide-footed elephant walks on soft ground. Same physics: pressure.
points: Fluids (liquids and gases) flow; they cannot resist a shear stress and take the shape of their container.
Liquids are nearly incompressible (fixed volume); gases are highly compressible.
Pressure P = F/A (normal force per unit area). It is a scalar; SI unit pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²).
Small area → large pressure (sharp knife, needle). Large area → small pressure (wide foundations, snowshoes, broad straps of a school bag).
Density ρ = m/V (kg m⁻³); water ≈ 1000 kg m⁻³, mercury ≈ 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Relative density = ρ/ρ_water (dimensionless).

example.q: A 60 kg girl stands on one heel of area 1 cm². Find the pressure on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²).

learn.reallife: Railway tracks rest on wide concrete sleepers so the enormous weight of a goods train is spread out and the ground doesn't sink.

topics.title: Pascal's law and pressure at depth

learn.hook: Divers in the Andaman Sea feel their ears pop just 3–4 m down. Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere of pressure.
points: Pascal's law: in a fluid at rest, pressure at a point is the same in all directions, and pressure is the same at all points at the same level (same depth).
Pressure at depth h below the open surface: P = P_a + ρgh, where P_a is atmospheric pressure.
The difference between two depths: P₂ − P₁ = ρg(h₂ − h₁).

Hydrostatic paradox: the pressure at the base depends only on the depth of liquid, not on the shape or volume of the vessel. Vessels of different shapes filled to the same height have equal pressure at the base.

example.q: Find the absolute pressure on a swimmer 10 m below the surface of a lake (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻², P_a = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa).

learn.reallife: Dams like Sardar Sarovar are built much thicker at the base because water pressure (and hence force per unit area) grows with depth.

topics.title: Atmospheric pressure, barometers and manometers

learn.hook: The air above you presses on your palm with the weight of about 100 kg! You don't feel it because the pressure acts on all sides.
points: Atmospheric pressure at sea level: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. It equals the pressure of a 76 cm (760 mm) column of mercury.
Torricelli's mercury barometer: a long tube of mercury inverted in a dish; mercury stands at h ≈ 76 cm, with near-vacuum above. P_a = ρgh. Units: 1 torr = 1 mm of Hg; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.
Open-tube manometer: a U-tube with liquid; the difference in levels h gives the gauge pressure: P − P_a = ρgh.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with height (air becomes thinner), roughly halving every 5–6 km near the Earth.

example.q: Show that 76 cm of mercury corresponds to about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa (ρ_Hg = 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

learn.reallife: Mountaineers on the way to Ladakh's Khardung La notice breathlessness and chips packets puffing up: the outside air pressure is much lower up there.

topics.title: Hydraulic machines and forces on dams

learn.hook: A mechanic in a garage lifts an SUV with one hand on a lever. The secret is Pascal's law of transmission of pressure.
points: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the walls (Pascal's law of transmission).
Hydraulic lift: pressure F₁/A₁ on the small piston appears at the large piston, giving F₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁). Force is multiplied by the area ratio.
Work is not multiplied: the small piston moves farther (d₁A₁ = d₂A₂).
Hydraulic brakes in cars use the same principle: a small push on the brake pedal produces large forces on the brake shoes of all wheels.
Typical problems: pressure on a swimmer at depth; force on a dam; two-piston lifts.

topics.title: Streamline flow and the equation of continuity

learn.hook: Press your thumb over a garden hose and the water shoots far. Narrow opening, faster flow: that's continuity.
points: Steady (streamline) flow: the velocity at each point does not change with time. Streamlines are the paths of fluid particles; they never cross.
A bundle of streamlines forms a flow tube. Above a critical speed, flow becomes turbulent (irregular, with eddies).
Equation of continuity (incompressible fluid, conservation of mass): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (volume flow rate is constant).
Where streamlines crowd together (narrower region), the fluid moves faster.

example.q: Water flows at 2 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of area 10 cm² that narrows to 4 cm². Find the speed in the narrow part.

learn.reallife: Rivers like the Ganga flow slowly where they are wide (near Varanasi's ghats) and rush through narrow gorges in the Himalayas.

topics.title: Bernoulli's principle

learn.hook: During a cyclone in Odisha, roofs are lifted off houses. Fast wind over the roof means low pressure above, while the air inside is still.
points: Bernoulli's principle: along a streamline, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant (for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow).
Derivation: apply the work–energy theorem to a fluid element in a tube of varying area and height. Work done by pressure forces = change in KE + change in gravitational PE.
Each term is energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy.
For a fluid at rest (v = 0), it reduces to P₁ − P₂ = ρg(h₂ − h₁), the pressure–depth relation.
Limitations: ignores viscosity (energy loss), compressibility and unsteady/turbulent flow.

example.q: Water flows horizontally through a pipe; speed changes from 2 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹. Find the pressure difference (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³).
steps: Same height, so P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².
= 6000 Pa (pressure is lower where the water is faster).

learn.reallife: The venturi in older scooter carburettors uses Bernoulli's principle: fast air in the narrow throat lowers pressure and sucks in petrol.

topics.title: Torricelli's law, dynamic lift and Bernoulli in action

learn.hook: A spin bowler makes the ball drift in the air; a passenger jet lifts hundreds of people off the runway at Delhi. Both are Bernoulli at work.
points: Speed of efflux (Torricelli's law): water from a small hole at depth h below the open surface of a large tank leaves at v = √(2gh), like a body falling freely through h.
Magnus effect: a spinning ball drags air around it; air moves faster on one side, so pressure is lower there and the ball swerves (dynamic lift).
Aerofoil (wing): air flows faster over the curved upper surface than below, so pressure above is lower; lift = ΔP × area = ½ρ(v_top² − v_bottom²)A.
Everyday effects: blowing over a strip of paper lifts it; an atomiser/spray uses fast air to suck liquid up; roofs are blown off in storms.

example.q: Air flows over a wing at 50 m s⁻¹ and under it at 40 m s⁻¹ (ρ = 1.2 kg m⁻³). Find the lift on a wing of area 20 m².

learn.reallife: Swing and drift in cricket owe a lot to air flow around the ball; spin bowlers use the Magnus effect to make the ball dip or drift.

topics.title: Viscosity

learn.hook: Pour honey and water side by side: water races, honey crawls. The difference is viscosity, the fluid's internal friction.
points: Viscosity is internal friction between layers of a fluid in relative motion; it opposes the relative motion of layers.
In laminar flow, layers slide over each other with a velocity gradient v/l. Coefficient of viscosity η = (F/A)/(v/l), i.e. shear stress/strain rate.
SI unit: Pa s (also N s m⁻²); CGS unit poise (1 poise = 0.1 Pa s). Honey and glycerine have large η; water and air small η.
Temperature: viscosity of liquids decreases as temperature rises; viscosity of gases increases with temperature.
Example: a plate dragged over a thin oil film: η = Fl/(Av).

example.q: A metal plate of area 0.1 m² is pulled at 0.5 m s⁻¹ over a 1 mm oil film with a force of 0.5 N. Find η.

learn.reallife: Engine oils sold at Indian petrol pumps are graded by viscosity (like 20W-40) so they flow in a cold Shimla winter and still protect in hot Chennai summers.

topics.title: Stokes' law and terminal velocity

learn.hook: Raindrops fall from clouds kilometres high but hit you gently. Air drag makes them stop accelerating and reach a steady terminal speed.
points: Stokes' law: a small sphere of radius a moving slowly at speed v through a fluid of viscosity η feels a drag force F = 6πηav.
As a sphere falls, drag grows with speed until weight = buoyancy + drag. Then acceleration is zero: terminal velocity v_t.
Balancing: (4/3)πa³ρg = (4/3)πa³σg + 6πηav_t gives v_t = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), where ρ is the sphere's density and σ the fluid's.
v_t ∝ a²: bigger drops fall faster. If ρ < σ (air bubble in water), v_t is negative: the bubble rises.

example.q: A steel ball falls in oil and reaches terminal velocity 2 cm s⁻¹. What would be the terminal velocity of a ball of the same material with twice the radius?

learn.reallife: Doctors at AIIMS use the Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) test: red blood cells settle at a nearly constant speed governed by Stokes-type drag. Lab safety: if you time steel balls falling through glycerine or oil, wipe up spills at once (the floor gets slippery) and drop the balls gently so the glass jar doesn't crack.

topics.title: Surface tension and surface energy

learn.hook: Water striders skate on ponds in Kerala's backwaters, and a steel needle can float on water. The surface acts like a stretched skin.
points: A liquid surface behaves like a stretched membrane. A molecule inside is pulled equally from all sides, but a surface molecule is pulled inward, so surface molecules have extra energy.
Surface energy: extra energy of the surface. To increase the surface area, work must be done.
Surface tension S = force per unit length acting along the surface, = surface energy per unit area (unit N m⁻¹ or J m⁻²).
Film on a wire frame with a movable slider of length l: the film has two surfaces, so F = 2Sl. Work to increase area by ΔA (each side) = S × 2ΔA.
Water at room temperature: S ≈ 0.072 N m⁻¹. Surface tension decreases as temperature rises.

example.q: A soap film (S = 0.03 N m⁻¹) is held on a frame with a movable slider of length 10 cm. Find the force needed to hold the slider.
steps: The film has two surfaces: F = 2Sl.

learn.reallife: Hot water and detergents clean oily dishes better because both reduce surface tension, helping water spread and wet the grease.

topics.title: Angle of contact and wetting

learn.hook: Water spreads on clean glass but beads up on a lotus leaf. The angle of contact decides whether a liquid wets a surface.
points: Angle of contact θ: the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid.
θ < 90°: the liquid wets the surface and spreads (water on clean glass, θ ≈ 0°). θ > 90°: the liquid does not wet it and forms drops (mercury on glass, water on wax or lotus leaves).
Balance of interfacial tensions at the edge: S_sa = S_la cos θ + S_sl (solid–air, liquid–air, solid–liquid).
If S_sl < S_sa, cos θ > 0 and θ is acute; if S_sl > S_sa, θ is obtuse.
Soaps and detergents lower the contact angle, so water wets cloth and grease better; waterproofing agents raise it.

example.q: For a liquid on a solid, S_sa = 0.05 N m⁻¹, S_sl = 0.02 N m⁻¹ and S_la = 0.06 N m⁻¹. Find cos θ and decide if the liquid wets the solid.
steps: θ = 60° < 90°, so the liquid wets the solid.

learn.reallife: Waterproof jackets used by trekkers in Meghalaya, one of the rainiest places on Earth, have coatings that make water's contact angle obtuse so it rolls off.

topics.title: Drops, bubbles and capillary rise

learn.hook: Plants pull water up through tiny tubes, and a cloth wick soaks up oil in a diya. Capillary action at work.
points: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop (one surface): Pᵢ − Pₒ = 2S/r. An air bubble inside a liquid also has one surface: 2S/r.
Soap bubble in air has two surfaces: Pᵢ − Pₒ = 4S/r. Smaller bubbles have larger excess pressure.
Capillary rise: h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr). Concave meniscus (θ < 90°, water in glass) rises; convex meniscus (θ > 90°, mercury) is depressed.
h ∝ 1/r: narrower tubes, higher rise.
Small drops are spherical because surface tension minimises the area; surface energy problems use W = S ΔA.

From the smaller bubble to the larger one

quiz.explain: Each surface contributes 2S/r.
quiz.mistake: Treats it like a liquid drop

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Water rises higher in a narrower capillary tube.
Reason (R): Capillary rise is directly proportional to the radius of the tube.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr) is inversely proportional to r.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why oil climbs up a diya's wick and why tiny soap bubbles are 'stronger'. Explain excess pressure and capillary rise.
teach.praise: Drops have 2S/r inside, soap bubbles 4S/r, and liquids climb narrow tubes by h = 2S cos θ/ρgr!
teach.nudge: What is the extra pressure inside a drop and a soap bubble? How does the tube's radius affect the rise?

topics.title: Temperature, heat and thermal equilibrium

learn.hook: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon in the same kitchen are at the same temperature, yet the steel one feels colder. Heat and temperature are not the same thing.
points: Thermal phenomena are everywhere: bodies get hot, expand, melt, boil and cool. To explain them we must separate heat from temperature.
Temperature is a relative measure of hotness or coldness of a body. SI unit: kelvin (K).
Heat is energy transferred from one system to another (or to its surroundings) because of a temperature difference. SI unit: joule (J).
Heat flows from higher to lower temperature until the temperatures are equal: the bodies are then in thermal equilibrium.
A body does not 'contain heat'; heat is energy in transit.

example.q: A glass of cold water (10 °C) is left in a room at 30 °C. Describe what happens.
steps: The room is hotter, so heat flows from the room into the water.
The water warms; the transfer slows as the difference shrinks.
It stops when the water reaches 30 °C: thermal equilibrium.
example.answer: Heat flows in until both are at 30 °C

learn.reallife: A chai seller's kulhad cools in the winter air of Lucknow as heat flows out of it until it reaches the air's temperature.

quiz.explain: Heat is energy, measured in joules (calorie is an older unit).

options: Equal heat can produce different temperature rises in different bodies
quiz.explain: The temperature rise depends on mass and material too.

teach.praise: Heat is energy on the move; temperature is how hot. Flow stops when temperatures match!
teach.nudge: Is heat the same as temperature? When does heat stop flowing?

topics.title: Thermometers and temperature scales

learn.hook: A doctor says 98.6 °F, the weather app says 37 °C. Same body temperature, two different scales.
points: A thermometer uses a property that changes regularly with temperature: expansion of a liquid (mercury, alcohol) or the pressure of a gas at constant volume.
Two fixed points define a scale: ice point (freezing of pure water) and steam point (boiling of pure water) at 1 atm.
Celsius: ice point 0 °C, steam point 100 °C. Fahrenheit: 32 °F and 212 °F (180 divisions).
Linear relation: (t_F − 32)/180 = t_C/100, i.e. t_F = (9/5)t_C + 32.
The two scales read the same at −40°.

example.q: Convert 37 °C into °F.

learn.reallife: IMD weather bulletins in India report temperatures in °C, while many older clinical thermometers in Indian homes are still marked in °F.

quiz.q: Convert 25 °C to °F.
Convert 104 °F to °C.
At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales give the same reading?
The number of divisions between the ice point and steam point on the Fahrenheit scale is
quiz.explain: 212 − 32 = 180 divisions.

quiz.q: A temperature change of 10 °C equals a change of (in °F)
quiz.explain: A change of 1 °C equals 9/5 °F, so 10 °C → 18 °F (the 32 does not enter for differences).

quiz.q: A thermometer works because
options: Some physical property of a substance changes regularly with temperature
quiz.explain: Expansion of liquids or gas pressure changes predictably with temperature.

quiz.q: A faulty thermometer reads 5° at the ice point and 95° at the steam point. When it reads 50°, the true temperature in °C is

Assertion (A): The relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures is linear.
Reason (R): Both scales are defined using the same two fixed points with uniform divisions between them.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Uniform scales with common fixed points must be linearly related. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu's thermometer shows 98.6 and he panics that he is boiling! Explain thermometers, fixed points and converting between °C and °F.
teach.praise: 98.6 °F is just 37 °C, a normal temperature! Use t_F = (9/5)t_C + 32.
teach.nudge: What are the fixed points of a scale? How do you convert between °C and °F?

topics.title: Gas laws, the ideal-gas equation and absolute temperature

learn.hook: Cool a gas at constant volume and its pressure falls in a straight line. Extend that line and it hits zero pressure at −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
points: Boyle's law: PV = constant at fixed T. Charles' law: V/T = constant at fixed P. Combined: PV = μRT (ideal-gas equation), μ = number of moles, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Constant-volume gas thermometer: at fixed volume, pressure varies linearly with temperature.
Extrapolating the P–t line to P = 0 (for any gas at low density) gives t = −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
Kelvin scale: T = t_C + 273.15. One kelvin equals one Celsius degree in size.
The triple point of water, 273.16 K, is used as the standard fixed point of the kelvin scale.

example.q: A gas at 27 °C and 2 atm is heated at constant volume until its pressure becomes 3 atm. Find the new temperature.
steps: At constant V, P/T is constant: T₂ = T₁ × P₂/P₁ = 300 × 3/2.

learn.reallife: Tyre pressures of trucks on the Mumbai–Ahmedabad highway rise on hot afternoons: same volume, higher temperature, higher pressure.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: All gases give the same intercept, −273.15 °C. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each gas gives a different absolute zero

teach.ask: Gappu asks, 'Why can't temperatures go below −273 °C?' Explain the gas laws, the gas thermometer and the kelvin scale.
teach.praise: Extend the gas's pressure line to zero and you hit −273.15 °C. That's 0 K, absolute zero!
teach.nudge: How does pressure change with temperature at constant volume? Where does that line hit zero pressure?

topics.title: Thermal expansion of solids

learn.hook: On a hot day, steel bridges like the Howrah Bridge grow a few centimetres longer. Engineers plan for it.
points: Most substances expand on heating: in length (linear), area (superficial) and volume (cubical).
Linear: ΔL = αLΔT, α = ΔL/(LΔT) (unit K⁻¹). Typical α: copper ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, aluminium ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹; glass and invar are much smaller.
Area: ΔA = α_A AΔT; volume: ΔV = α_V VΔT.
For isotropic solids: α_A = 2α and α_V = 3α.
A hole in a plate expands on heating as if it were made of the plate material. Measuring tapes and rods read wrong at temperatures other than their calibration temperature.

example.q: A 10 m copper wire (α = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is heated by 50 K. Find the increase in length.

learn.reallife: Blacksmiths in Moradabad heat iron rims before fitting them on cart wheels; the rim shrinks on cooling and grips tightly.

quiz.q: A 2 m aluminium rod (α = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 120 °C. Its increase in length in mm is

quiz.explain: V = L³ → ΔV/V = 3ΔL/L.

quiz.q: A circular hole in a metal plate is heated. The hole's diameter
quiz.explain: The plate expands uniformly, like a photographic enlargement; the hole grows too.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the metal expands into the hole

quiz.q: A metal sheet has α = 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Its area expansion coefficient in units of 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ is
A steel tape calibrated at 20 °C is used at 40 °C to measure a length. Its readings will be
options: Slightly smaller than the true length
Slightly larger than the true length
quiz.explain: The tape's markings spread apart when hot, so each 'metre' on it is longer and fewer fit along the object.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a hot tape reads larger

quiz.explain: α = ΔL/(LΔT): m/(m K) = K⁻¹.

Assertion (A): For an isotropic solid, α_V = 3α.
Reason (R): The coefficient of linear expansion is measured in K⁻¹.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the unit does not explain the factor 3; equal expansion in three directions does.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true but irrelevant fact

teach.ask: Gappu notices the metal gate in his garden sticks in summer. Explain linear, area and volume expansion and how they are related.
teach.praise: Heat makes metals grow: ΔL = αLΔT, area by 2α, volume by 3α. Even holes get bigger!
teach.nudge: How does length change with temperature? How are area and volume expansion related to α?

topics.title: Expansion of liquids and gases, and water's strange behaviour

learn.hook: Lakes in Kashmir freeze from the top down in winter, and fish survive below. Water's anomalous expansion makes it possible.
points: Liquids and gases have only volume expansion; liquids generally expand more than solids, gases much more.
For an ideal gas at constant pressure, PV = μRT gives α_V = 1/T. At 0 °C (273 K), α_V ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, far larger than for solids or liquids.
Anomalous expansion of water: from 0 °C to 4 °C, water CONTRACTS on heating; above 4 °C it expands. So water is densest at 4 °C.

In winter, surface water cools, becomes denser and sinks until the whole lake is at 4 °C. Further cooling makes the surface lighter; it freezes at the top, and the ice layer insulates the water below, letting aquatic life survive.

example.q: Find the coefficient of volume expansion of an ideal gas at constant pressure at 27 °C.

learn.reallife: The Dal Lake surface freezes in harsh winters, but water at about 4 °C below the ice keeps fish alive till spring.

teach.praise: Water is densest at 4 °C, so the lake freezes on top and the ice blanket keeps the fish safe!
teach.nudge: At what temperature is water densest? Why does ice form on top?

topics.title: Thermal stress and uses of expansion

learn.hook: A steel rail clamped tight on a summer afternoon can buckle with tremendous force. That's why old tracks had small gaps.
points: If a rod is prevented from expanding, a thermal stress develops: strain = αΔT, so thermal stress = YαΔT, and force = YAαΔT.
Example: a steel rail (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) clamped at both ends and heated by 20 K develops stress 2 × 10¹¹ × 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 20 = 4.8 × 10⁷ Pa.

Applications: gaps between rail sections, expansion joints in bridges; bimetallic strips (two metals with different α bend on heating) in thermostats and fire alarms; heating iron rims to fit on wheels.

example.q: A brass rod (Y = 10¹¹ Pa, α = 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, area 10⁻⁴ m²) is clamped between rigid walls and heated by 50 K. Find the stress and the force on the walls.

learn.reallife: Modern Indian Railways tracks use long welded rails pre-stressed at a chosen temperature, plus special joints, to manage thermal stress.

topics.title: Heat capacity and specific heat

learn.hook: Coastal Chennai has milder temperature swings than inland Nagpur. The sea's huge heat capacity acts like a giant thermal buffer.
points: Heat capacity of a body S = ΔQ/ΔT (unit J K⁻¹): heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 K.
Specific heat capacity s = ΔQ/(mΔT), unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. It depends on the substance and (slightly) on temperature.
Molar specific heat C = ΔQ/(μΔT), unit J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
For gases, heat capacity depends on the conditions: C_p (constant pressure) > C_v (constant volume), because at constant pressure some heat goes into doing work.
Water has a very high specific heat (≈ 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). So it heats and cools slowly, moderates coastal climates, and is an excellent coolant in car radiators.

example.q: How much heat raises 2 kg of water from 25 °C to 75 °C? (s = 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

learn.reallife: Car radiators use water-based coolant because water absorbs a lot of heat with only a small temperature rise.

At constant volume the gas does more work
quiz.explain: At constant V no work is done, so all heat raises U; at constant P some goes into work.

teach.ask: Gappu notices the beach sand burns his feet at noon but the sea water feels cool. Explain heat capacity and specific heat.

teach.nudge: What does specific heat measure? Why does water heat up slowly?

topics.title: Calorimetry and the method of mixtures

learn.hook: Mix hot and cold water in a bucket for a bath and you instinctively do calorimetry: heat lost by one equals heat gained by the other.
points: A calorimeter (often a copper vessel with a stirrer, inside an insulated jacket) keeps the system isolated so no heat is lost to the surroundings.
Principle of method of mixtures: heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body (and the calorimeter).
m₁s₁(T₁ − T) = m₂s₂(T − T₂) + m_c s_c(T − T₂), where T is the final common temperature.
Use it to find an unknown specific heat or a final temperature.

example.q: 0.2 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.3 kg of water at 20 °C (ignore the container). Find the final temperature.
steps: Heat lost = heat gained: 0.2 × s × (80 − T) = 0.3 × s × (T − 20).

learn.reallife: In BIS testing labs, the specific heat of materials like cookware metals is found using the method of mixtures in calorimeters. Lab safety: lift the hot metal with tongs, transfer it quickly over the bench (not over your hands), and never touch the steam heater or boiling water.

When hot and cold water are mixed in a perfectly insulated vessel, the final temperature

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The final temperature of a mixture of 1 kg water at 80 °C and 3 kg water at 20 °C is 50 °C.
Reason (R): Heat lost by the hot water equals the heat gained by the cold water.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

teach.ask: Gappu mixed hot and cold water and wants to predict the final temperature. Teach him calorimetry.

teach.nudge: What is equal in a mixture inside a calorimeter? Which formula do you use for each part?

topics.title: Change of state: melting, boiling and sublimation

learn.hook: Dal takes longer to cook in Leh than in Delhi. At high altitude, water boils at a lower temperature, so food cooks slower.
points: Changes of state: melting/fusion (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), vaporisation/boiling (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), sublimation (solid → gas directly).
During a change of state, temperature stays constant even though heat is supplied; the heating curve of water shows flat steps at 0 °C and 100 °C.

Melting point decreases with increase of pressure for ice. Regelation: a weighted wire passes through an ice block (ice melts under the wire and refreezes above it); ice skating works partly this way.
Boiling point increases with pressure: it is lower at high altitudes and higher in a pressure cooker (about 120 °C).
Sublimation: dry ice (solid CO₂), iodine, naphthalene. At the triple point (water: 273.16 K), solid, liquid and vapour coexist.

example.q: Ice at −10 °C is heated steadily until it becomes steam at 110 °C. Describe the temperature–time graph.

learn.reallife: Pressure cookers in Indian kitchens raise the boiling point of water to about 120 °C, cooking rajma and chana much faster.

topics.title: Latent heat

learn.hook: A burn from steam at 100 °C is far worse than one from boiling water at 100 °C. Latent heat is the hidden culprit.
points: Heat needed to change the state of mass m without changing temperature: Q = mL, where L is the latent heat (J kg⁻¹).
Water: latent heat of fusion L_f ≈ 3.33 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; latent heat of vaporisation L_v ≈ 22.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
Steam at 100 °C releases its large latent heat (2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) on condensing on the skin, then more as the water cools, so it burns worse than water at 100 °C.
Ice at −t °C to steam: add the heats msΔT (ice) + mL_f + msΔT (water) + mL_v.
Mixing ice with warm water: first check whether all the ice can melt; if the heat available is less than mL_f, the final temperature is 0 °C with some ice left.

example.q: Find the heat needed to turn 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C, and then into steam at 100 °C (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵, L_v = 22.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, s = 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Matka water stays cool in Rajasthan summers because water seeping through the clay evaporates and takes away latent heat.

topics.title: Conduction of heat

learn.hook: Steel cooking pots often have copper bottoms. Copper conducts heat many times better than steel, spreading the flame's heat evenly.
points: Heat is transferred by three modes: conduction, convection and radiation.
Conduction: heat flows through a material from hot to cold regions by molecular collisions, without bulk movement. Heat current H = KA(T_C − T_D)/L.
K is the thermal conductivity (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Metals are good conductors (copper ≈ 400); wood, glass and especially gases (air ≈ 0.024) are poor conductors (insulators).
Uses: copper-bottomed pots; insulating materials (glass wool, air gaps) in buildings and flasks; ice on lakes conducts poorly and protects water below.
Rods in series at steady state: the same heat current flows through each: K₁A(T₁ − T)/L₁ = K₂A(T − T₂)/L₂.

example.q: Two rods of equal length and area are joined end to end. Rod A (K = 3K₀) is at 100 °C at its free end, rod B (K = K₀) is at 0 °C at its free end. Find the junction temperature.

learn.reallife: Traditional mud-and-thatch houses in rural India stay cool because mud and straw are poor conductors of heat.

topics.title: Convection and radiation

learn.hook: At Marina Beach, the afternoon breeze blows in from the sea; at night it reverses. That's convection on a giant scale.
points: Convection: heat transfer by actual (bulk) movement of a fluid. Natural convection is driven by density differences under gravity (hot fluid rises); forced convection uses a pump or fan.

Sea breeze (day): land heats faster, warm air over land rises, cooler air from the sea flows in. Land breeze (night): the reverse. Trade winds arise from convection between the hot equator and cooler regions, deflected by Earth's rotation.
Radiation: heat transfer by electromagnetic waves; needs no medium (the Sun's heat crosses empty space). It travels at the speed of light.
Good absorbers are good emitters. A black body absorbs all radiation falling on it. Dark clothes absorb more heat; white clothes reflect more.
Thermos flask: double glass walls with vacuum between (cuts conduction and convection), silvered surfaces (cut radiation).

example.q: Explain why a land breeze blows at night.
steps: At night, land cools faster than the sea (lower specific heat).
Air over the sea is warmer and rises.
Cooler air from the land flows towards the sea: a land breeze.
example.answer: Land cools faster; air flows from land to sea

learn.reallife: White kurtas in Rajasthan summers and dark blankets in Himachal winters use the physics of absorption and reflection of radiation.
