topics.title: Blackbody radiation: Wien's and Stefan's laws

learn.hook: Astronomers at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics tell a star's surface temperature just by its colour. Wien's law makes it possible.
points: A black body emits radiation over all wavelengths; the energy distribution with wavelength depends only on its temperature.
Wien's displacement law: λ_m T = b, with b ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. Hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths (red → white → blue-hot).
The Sun's spectrum peaks near 480–500 nm, giving a surface temperature of about 6000 K.
Stefan–Boltzmann law: power radiated H = σAT⁴ (black body), H = eσAT⁴ for a real body with emissivity e (0 ≤ e ≤ 1). σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
Net loss to surroundings at T_s: H_net = eσA(T⁴ − T_s⁴).

example.q: A star's radiation peaks at λ_m = 290 nm. Estimate its surface temperature.

learn.reallife: Thermal cameras used by Indian Army border patrols detect people at night because warm bodies radiate infrared strongly (λ_m ≈ 10 µm at body temperature).

topics.title: Newton's law of cooling

learn.hook: Your chai cools from 90 °C to 70 °C quickly, but from 40 °C to 35 °C painfully slowly. Newton's law of cooling explains the slowdown.
points: For small temperature differences, the rate of loss of heat is proportional to the difference between the body and its surroundings.
dT/dt = −k(T − T_s), where k depends on the surface area and nature of the body. The temperature difference decays exponentially with time.
Approximate method for intervals: average rate (ΔT/Δt) ∝ (average temperature − T_s).
Lab activity: heat water in a calorimeter, record temperature every minute while it cools, and plot T against t (falling curve) and log(T − T_s) against t (straight line) to verify the law.
Typical numericals combine expansion, calorimetry, latent heat, conduction and cooling.

example.q: A body cools from 90 °C to 70 °C in 5 min in a room at 20 °C. How long will it take to cool from 70 °C to 50 °C?
steps: First interval: rate = 20/5 = 4 °C/min at average 80 °C (difference 60): 4 = k × 60 → k = 1/15 per min.

learn.reallife: Hospital labs in India store blood samples in insulated boxes; Newton's law of cooling helps estimate how long the samples stay within the safe temperature range. Lab safety: pour hot water slowly, hold the calorimeter by its insulated jacket, and read the thermometer without lifting it out.

topics.title: Thermodynamic systems and thermal equilibrium

learn.hook: A pressure cooker on a gas stove: heat goes in, steam pushes the weight up, work gets done. Thermodynamics is the science of exactly this.
points: Thermodynamics studies heat, temperature and the conversion of heat into work and vice versa, for macroscopic systems.
It uses macroscopic variables such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass and composition, not the motion of individual molecules (which is the microscopic description of kinetic theory).
A system is the part of the universe under study; everything else is the surroundings. Walls can be adiabatic (insulating: no heat flow) or diathermic (conducting: heat can flow).
A system is in equilibrium when its macroscopic variables do not change with time.
Two systems separated by a diathermic wall reach thermal equilibrium when their temperatures become equal and no further change happens.

example.q: Gas A at 400 K and gas B at 300 K are in a box with a partition. What happens if the partition is (a) adiabatic (b) diathermic?
steps: (a) Adiabatic: no heat flows; each gas keeps its own state.
(b) Diathermic: heat flows from A to B.
Their pressures and volumes adjust until temperatures are equal: thermal equilibrium.
example.answer: (a) No change (b) They reach a common temperature

topics.title: Zeroth law and internal energy

learn.hook: When a doctor reads your fever from a thermometer, she relies on the zeroth law: you and the thermometer reach thermal equilibrium.
points: Zeroth law: if two systems A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
This law tells us there is a quantity that is equal for systems in thermal equilibrium: temperature. It makes thermometers meaningful.
Internal energy U of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules, measured in the frame where the system's centre of mass is at rest.
Bulk kinetic energy of the whole system (e.g. a moving gas container) is NOT part of its internal energy.
For an ideal gas, molecular interactions are negligible, so U is purely kinetic and depends only on temperature.

example.q: A thermometer C reads 37 °C when touching A and also 37 °C when touching B. Are A and B in thermal equilibrium?
steps: A is in thermal equilibrium with C.
B is in thermal equilibrium with C.
By the zeroth law, A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other (same temperature).

topics.title: Heat, work and the first law

learn.hook: Rub your palms together and they warm up; put a lid on boiling water and it rattles. Heat and work are two ways to change internal energy.
points: Internal energy U is a state variable: it depends only on the state (P, V, T), not on how the state was reached. Heat and work are NOT state variables; they depend on the process.
Energy can be transferred to a gas in a cylinder by heating it (heat) or by pushing the piston (work).
First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW. Heat supplied to a system is used partly to increase its internal energy and partly to do work. It is the law of conservation of energy for thermodynamic systems.
Sign convention (NCERT): ΔQ > 0 when heat is supplied TO the system; ΔW > 0 when work is done BY the system; ΔU > 0 when internal energy increases.

example.q: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings. Find ΔU.
steps: ΔQ = +500 J (heat supplied); ΔW = +200 J (work by the gas).

learn.reallife: The diesel engines of Indian Railways' WDM locomotives convert fuel's heat into work; the first law tracks every joule.

topics.title: Work at constant pressure and boiling water

learn.hook: When water boils in an open pot, it pushes back the atmosphere as it turns into steam. A part of the heat you supply goes into that push.
points: Work done by a gas expanding at constant pressure P: ΔW = PΔV.
Boiling water at 1 atm: heat supplied ΔQ = mL; work done against the atmosphere ΔW = PΔV (ΔV = steam volume − water volume); increase in internal energy ΔU = ΔQ − ΔW.
Most of the latent heat goes into internal energy (breaking intermolecular bonds); a smaller part does work pushing back the air.
Work is positive for expansion, negative for compression.

example.q: 2 g of water at 100 °C boils into steam at P = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa (L = 2260 J g⁻¹); the volume increases by 3.4 × 10⁻³ m³. Find ΔW and ΔU.

learn.reallife: A pressure cooker's whistle lifts because the steam does work PΔV pushing the weight up.

topics.title: Specific heat of solids and water, and the calorie

learn.hook: Copper, aluminium and lead have very different specific heats per kilogram, but per mole they are all close to 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Coincidence? No: energy sharing.
points: Specific heat capacity s = ΔQ/(mΔT); molar specific heat C = ΔQ/(μΔT).

For solids, each atom oscillates about its position with both kinetic and potential energy. Using equipartition: average energy per atom = 3k_BT, so U = 3RT per mole and C = 3R ≈ 24.9 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (Dulong–Petit law).
Experimental values agree well at ordinary temperatures (C is lower for some light, hard solids such as carbon and at low temperatures).
Water's specific heat is about 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The calorie is the heat that raises 1 g of water by 1 °C (14.5 °C to 15.5 °C): 1 cal = 4.186 J.
Mechanical equivalent of heat: J = 4.186 J cal⁻¹ (Joule showed work and heat are equivalent).

example.q: Using the Dulong–Petit law, estimate the heat needed to raise 2 mol of copper by 10 K (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Food labels in Indian supermarkets list energy in kcal; 1 kcal = 4186 J, the same calorie you meet in physics.

teach.praise: Each atom shares energy 3k_BT, so every mole needs about 3R per kelvin! And 1 cal = 4.186 J.
teach.nudge: Why do different solids have similar molar heat capacities? What is a calorie in joules?

topics.title: Cp, Cv and Mayer's relation

learn.hook: Heat a gas in a sealed steel can and in a balloon: the balloon needs more heat for the same temperature rise. The difference is exactly R per mole.
points: Molar specific heat at constant volume C_v: heat per mole per kelvin with V fixed (no work done).
Molar specific heat at constant pressure C_p: heat per mole per kelvin with P fixed (gas expands and does work).
Mayer's relation for an ideal gas: C_p − C_v = R.
Derivation: at constant V, ΔQ = ΔU = μC_vΔT. At constant P, ΔQ = ΔU + PΔV = μC_vΔT + μRΔT (since PΔV = μRΔT). So C_p = C_v + R.
γ = C_p/C_v > 1. For a monatomic gas C_v = 3R/2, C_p = 5R/2, γ = 5/3; for a diatomic gas (rigid) C_v = 5R/2, C_p = 7R/2, γ = 7/5.

example.q: For 2 mol of an ideal monatomic gas heated by 10 K, find the heat needed at constant volume and at constant pressure (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Engineers designing gas turbines at BHEL Hyderabad use C_p and γ of air to predict temperatures in compressors and turbines.

So μC_pΔT = μC_vΔT + μRΔT → C_p − C_v = R

topics.title: State variables, equation of state and quasi-static processes

learn.hook: Two ways to compress a gas: slam the piston or ease it in over minutes. Only the slow one keeps the gas in equilibrium at every step.
points: Equilibrium states are described by state variables such as P, V, T and U. A relation among them is the equation of state.
For an ideal gas the equation of state is PV = μRT.
Extensive variables depend on the size of the system (volume, mass, internal energy). Intensive variables do not (pressure, temperature, density).
A quasi-static process is infinitely slow, so the system passes through a series of equilibrium states; P and T are well defined at every stage and differ only infinitesimally from the surroundings.

example.q: A box of gas at P, V, T is divided into two equal halves by a partition. Which variables stay the same in each half?
steps: Intensive variables P and T (and density) are unchanged.
Extensive variables V, mass and U are halved.
example.answer: P, T, density unchanged; V, m, U halved

learn.reallife: Slowly pumping a bicycle tyre is closer to quasi-static than a sudden bang; that's why ideal-process formulas apply better to gentle changes.

topics.title: Isothermal and adiabatic processes

learn.hook: Pump a bicycle tyre fast and the pump gets hot: nearly adiabatic compression. Do it slowly in contact with air: closer to isothermal.
points: Isothermal (T constant): PV = constant. For an ideal gas, ΔU = 0, so ΔQ = ΔW.
Work in isothermal expansion: W = μRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 2.303 μRT log₁₀(V₂/V₁). Heat absorbed equals work done.
Adiabatic (ΔQ = 0, insulated or very fast): PV^γ = constant (also TV^(γ−1) = constant). W = μR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1). Expansion cools the gas; compression heats it.
On a P–V diagram, an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal curve through the same point (slope ratio γ).
Typical comparisons: for the same compression from the same state, adiabatic compression needs more work and ends at a higher pressure and temperature.

example.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally to twice its volume (R = 8.31, ln 2 = 0.693). Find the work done and the heat absorbed.

learn.reallife: Diesel engines in trucks ignite fuel without spark plugs: rapid (nearly adiabatic) compression heats the air above the fuel's ignition point.

topics.title: Isochoric, isobaric and cyclic processes

learn.hook: An engine's cylinder goes through a cycle again and again. The work it delivers each cycle is simply the area enclosed on a P–V graph.
points: Isochoric (V constant): W = 0; heat supplied changes only U and T: ΔQ = ΔU = μC_vΔT.
Isobaric (P constant): W = P(V₂ − V₁) = μR(T₂ − T₁); ΔQ = μC_pΔT.
Cyclic process: the system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and net heat absorbed = net work done = area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram (clockwise loop: positive work by the gas).
Comparisons: for compression from the same state to the same volume, adiabatic needs more work than isothermal.
Reading indicator (P–V) diagrams: vertical line = isochoric, horizontal line = isobaric, hyperbola = isothermal, steeper curve = adiabatic.

example.q: A gas goes round a rectangular cycle on a P–V diagram: P from 1 × 10⁵ to 3 × 10⁵ Pa and V from 1 × 10⁻³ to 4 × 10⁻³ m³ (clockwise). Find the net work.
steps: Clockwise loop: 600 J of net work done by the gas (= net heat absorbed).

learn.reallife: The indicator diagrams of steam engines in old Indian Railways workshops were literally drawn by a pen on the cylinder to measure work per cycle.

topics.title: The second law of thermodynamics

learn.hook: A cup of tea never spontaneously heats itself by cooling the room. The first law wouldn't object, but the second law forbids it.
points: The first law allows many processes that never happen (e.g. heat flowing by itself from cold to hot, or a hot body converting all its internal energy to work). The second law rules them out.
Kelvin–Planck statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and the complete conversion of this heat into work.
Clausius statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the transfer of heat from a colder object to a hotter object.
The two statements are equivalent: violating one would let us violate the other.
Consequence: no heat engine can have 100% efficiency; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir.

example.q: An inventor claims an engine that takes 1000 J from a hot reservoir and does 1000 J of work each cycle, rejecting nothing. Is this possible?
steps: That means heat fully converted into work with no other effect.
This violates the Kelvin–Planck statement, so it is impossible.
example.answer: No, it violates the second law

learn.reallife: Every power plant in India, coal or nuclear, rejects a large part of its heat to cooling towers and rivers because of the second law.

teach.nudge: What do the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements say? Why can't efficiency be 100%?

topics.title: Reversible and irreversible processes

learn.hook: Drop ink into water and it spreads; it never gathers itself back into a drop. Most real processes run only one way.
points: A reversible process can be retraced so that both the system and the surroundings return to their original states, with no other change in the universe.
Reversible processes must be quasi-static and free of dissipative effects; they are idealisations.
Irreversibility arises from dissipative effects (friction, viscosity, electrical resistance) and from non-quasi-static changes (sudden, far from equilibrium).
Examples of irreversible processes: free expansion of a gas into vacuum, heat flow across a finite temperature difference, mixing of two gases, a block sliding to rest by friction.

example.q: Is the free expansion of a gas into a vacuum reversible?
steps: The gas rushes into the empty half; the process is sudden, not quasi-static.
To return it, an external agent must compress the gas, which changes the surroundings.
So the system and surroundings cannot both be restored: irreversible.

learn.reallife: The brakes of a Delhi Metro train convert kinetic energy to heat by friction (irreversible), while its regenerative braking recovers part of it as electrical energy.

teach.nudge: What must happen for a process to be reversible? What makes most real processes irreversible?

topics.title: Heat engines and the Carnot cycle

learn.hook: Every car engine, steam turbine and thermal power plant follows the same plan: take heat from hot, do work, dump the rest to cold.
points: A heat engine uses a working substance that absorbs heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir (T₁), does work W, and rejects heat Q₂ to a cold reservoir (T₂) in a cycle. Efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.
A Carnot engine is an ideal reversible engine working between two temperatures T₁ and T₂.

Carnot cycle (four reversible steps): (1) isothermal expansion at T₁, absorbing Q₁; (2) adiabatic expansion, T₁ → T₂; (3) isothermal compression at T₂, rejecting Q₂; (4) adiabatic compression, T₂ → T₁.
On a P–V diagram: two isotherms and two adiabats. Net work = area enclosed. Heat flows only in the isothermal steps; in the adiabatic steps work changes the temperature.

example.q: An engine absorbs 1000 J from the hot reservoir and rejects 600 J to the cold reservoir per cycle. Find W and η.

learn.reallife: NTPC's thermal power stations are huge heat engines: coal burning gives the hot reservoir, and rivers or cooling towers provide the cold reservoir.

teach.nudge: What does a heat engine take in and give out? What are the four steps of the Carnot cycle?

topics.title: Carnot efficiency and Carnot's theorem

learn.hook: Even a perfect engine between 500 K steam and 300 K river water cannot beat 40% efficiency. Carnot set that ceiling in 1824.
points: For a Carnot engine: Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁, so η = 1 − T₂/T₁ (temperatures in kelvin).
Efficiency increases with a hotter source or a colder sink; it can reach 1 only if T₂ = 0 K, which is unattainable.
Carnot's theorem: (a) no engine working between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine; (b) the efficiency of a Carnot engine is independent of the working substance.
Problem types: first law, specific heats, work in processes, and Carnot efficiency.

example.q: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K and absorbs 1000 J per cycle. Find η, W and Q₂.

learn.reallife: Improving Indian thermal plants to 'supercritical' steam temperatures raises T₁, which raises the Carnot limit and cuts coal use per unit of electricity.

teach.praise: Efficiency only depends on T₁ and T₂ in kelvin. No gas, however clever, can beat Carnot!
teach.nudge: What decides the efficiency of a Carnot engine? Can any engine do better?

topics.title: Kinetic theory and the molecular nature of matter

learn.hook: You can't see air molecules, yet the pressure in your bicycle tyre is just billions of them drumming on the rubber every second.
points: Kinetic theory explains the behaviour of gases from the motion of their molecules: a gas is a swarm of rapidly moving molecules, and pressure and temperature come from that motion. Boyle, Newton, Maxwell and Boltzmann helped build it.
Atomic hypothesis: matter is made of tiny particles. Kanada in ancient India and Democritus in ancient Greece proposed indivisible constituents of matter.
Dalton's atomic theory explained the laws of definite and multiple proportions in chemistry.
Gay-Lussac's law: gases combine in simple ratios by volume. Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

example.q: 2 L of hydrogen combine with 1 L of oxygen to give 2 L of water vapour (same T and P). How does Avogadro's law explain this?
steps: Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules.
So 2 molecules of H₂ react with 1 molecule of O₂ to give 2 molecules of H₂O.
The simple volume ratio 2 : 1 : 2 reflects the molecular ratio.

learn.reallife: The Vaisheshika school of ancient Indian philosophy, associated with Kanada, described matter as made of 'paramanu', tiny eternal particles.

topics.title: Molecular spacing and the ideal gas equation

learn.hook: One mole of water is about 18 mL as a liquid, but over 30 litres as steam at 100 °C. Molecules in gases are far apart.
points: In solids, atoms are tightly packed (~2 Å apart); in liquids slightly farther; in gases the spacing is about ten times larger and interactions are weak.

Atoms are always in motion. In a liquid–vapour system in a closed container, molecules leave and return at equal rates: dynamic equilibrium. A molecule in a gas travels a certain average distance between collisions (the mean free path).
Ideal gas equation: PV = μRT = Nk_BT, where μ = number of moles, N = number of molecules, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
Avogadro's number N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. At STP (273 K, 1 atm), 1 mole of any gas occupies about 22.4 L.

example.q: How many molecules are there in 11.2 L of a gas at STP?

learn.reallife: LPG cylinders in Indian kitchens hold gas as a compressed liquid; when released it expands hugely because gas molecules are far apart.

topics.title: Gas laws, real gases and partial pressures

learn.hook: A scuba diver's tank holds a mix of gases, and each gas contributes its own share of the pressure. That's Dalton's law.
points: Boyle's law (PV constant at fixed T and μ) and Charles' law (V ∝ T at fixed P and μ) are special cases of PV = μRT.
Real gases follow the ideal gas law closely only at low pressures and high temperatures (molecules far apart, weak interactions).
Dalton's law of partial pressures: in a mixture of ideal gases, P = P₁ + P₂ + …, where each partial pressure Pᵢ = μᵢRT/V is the pressure that gas would exert alone.
Molecular volume fraction: in water vapour at 100 °C (ρ ≈ 0.6 kg m⁻³), molecules take up only ρ_vapour/ρ_liquid ≈ 0.6/1000 = 6 × 10⁻⁴ of the volume.

topics.title: Kinetic theory: assumptions and pressure

learn.hook: Picture a cricket ball hitting a wall again and again. A gas is that, with trillions of tiny balls every microsecond.
points: Assumptions: molecules are point-like (negligible size), move randomly, collide elastically with each other and the walls, and exert no forces except during collisions.
A molecule of mass m with velocity component vₓ hitting a wall transfers momentum 2mvₓ. Counting the molecules that hit in time Δt gives P = n m vₓ² (average).
Isotropy: random motion means vₓ² = v_y² = v_z² = v²/3 (averages), so P = (1/3) n m v̄², where n = number density and v̄² is the mean of the squared speed.
Pressure is the same in all directions (Pascal's law) because molecular motion is random.
Mixture: each gas contributes (1/3)nᵢm v̄ᵢ², so the total pressure is the sum of partial pressures (Dalton's law).

example.q: A gas has number density 2.5 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, molecular mass 5 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and mean square speed 2.4 × 10⁵ m² s⁻². Find its pressure.

learn.reallife: Weather balloons launched by IMD expand as they rise because outside molecular bombardment (pressure) drops with height.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders how invisible molecules create the pressure in his balloon. Explain the assumptions of kinetic theory and how pressure arises.

teach.nudge: What do molecules do to the walls? What formula gives the pressure?

topics.title: Temperature, kinetic energy and rms speed

learn.hook: Oxygen molecules in the air of your classroom zip around at nearly 500 m s⁻¹, faster than a passenger jet!
points: From P = (1/3)nmv̄² and PV = Nk_BT: average translational KE per molecule = ½m v̄² = (3/2)k_BT. Temperature is a measure of average molecular kinetic energy.
Total translational KE E of a gas: PV = (2/3)E.
Root mean square speed: v_rms = √(v̄²) = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M), M = molar mass in kg mol⁻¹.
At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster: v_rms ∝ 1/√M. E.g. v_rms(H₂) = 4 × v_rms(O₂).
Isotope separation: ²³⁵UF₆ and ²³⁸UF₆ have rms speeds in the ratio √(352/349) ≈ 1.0043; the slight difference in diffusion rates is used to enrich uranium.

topics.title: Degrees of freedom and equipartition of energy

learn.hook: A helium atom can only zip around; an oxygen molecule can also tumble. Every extra way to store energy changes how much heat a gas needs.
points: Degrees of freedom: independent ways a molecule can have energy. Translational (3 for motion along x, y, z), rotational, vibrational.
Monatomic molecule (He, Ar): 3 translational degrees of freedom. Rigid diatomic molecule (O₂, N₂): 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5.
A vibrational mode has both kinetic and potential energy, so it contributes two quadratic terms (2 × ½k_BT = k_BT).

Law of equipartition of energy: in thermal equilibrium, each quadratic energy term (each translational and rotational degree of freedom, and each of the two terms of a vibrational mode) has average energy ½k_BT per molecule.

example.q: Find the average energy of a rigid diatomic molecule at temperature T, and the energy of 1 mol.

learn.reallife: Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of the air we breathe in Delhi or Kochi, behave as rigid diatomic gases at room temperature.

topics.title: Specific heats of gases from equipartition

learn.hook: Measured C_v for helium is 12.5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and for nitrogen about 20.8. Equipartition predicts both numbers almost perfectly.
points: Rigid diatomic: U = (5/2)RT, C_v = (5/2)R, C_p = (7/2)R, γ = 7/5 = 1.4. With vibration also active: C_v = (7/2)R, C_p = (9/2)R, γ = 9/7.
Polyatomic (3 translational, 3 rotational, f vibrational modes): C_v = (3 + f)R, C_p = (4 + f)R, γ = (4 + f)/(3 + f).
Predicted values agree well with measurements for monatomic and many diatomic gases at room temperature (e.g. He ≈ 12.5, N₂ ≈ 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

steps: C_p = C_v + R = (7/2)R = 29.09 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

topics.title: Specific heat of solids and gas mixtures

learn.hook: At room temperature most solids need about 25 J to warm one mole by 1 K, but near absolute zero that number plunges. Classical physics can't explain why.
points: Solids: each atom oscillates in 3 dimensions. Each direction has KE and PE terms: 2 × ½k_BT per direction, so 3k_BT per atom.
Hence U = 3RT per mole and C = 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (Dulong–Petit law). At constant pressure and volume the values are nearly equal for solids.
At low temperatures, specific heats of solids (and the vibrational part for gases) fall below classical values. Explaining this needs quantum ideas (energy comes in discrete amounts).
Gas mixtures: C_v(mix) = (μ₁C_v1 + μ₂C_v2)/(μ₁ + μ₂). Heat for a gas in a cylinder: Q = μC_vΔT (rigid) or μC_pΔT (constant pressure).

example.q: Find C_v of a mixture of 1 mol of helium and 1 mol of oxygen (rigid).

learn.reallife: Cryogenic engines developed by ISRO handle materials near very low temperatures, where specific heats are far below the room-temperature 3R values.

topics.title: Mean free path

learn.hook: Gas molecules move at hundreds of metres per second, yet a smell takes minutes to cross a room. They keep bumping into each other.
points: Mean free path l: the average distance a molecule travels between successive collisions.
l = 1/(√2 n π d²), where n is the number density and d the molecular diameter.
l decreases if the gas is denser (larger n) or the molecules are bigger (larger d). l ∝ 1/n, so at constant T, l ∝ 1/P.
Collision frequency ≈ v̄/l; time between collisions ≈ l/v̄. For air at STP, l ≈ 10⁻⁷ m, much larger than the molecular size (~10⁻¹⁰ m) and than the spacing (~3 × 10⁻⁹ m).
Typical estimates: average spacing (1/n)^(1/3), mean free path, and rms speed at a given temperature.

example.q: Molecules of diameter d = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m have number density n = 2 × 10²⁵ m⁻³. Estimate the mean free path (π ≈ 3.14, √2 ≈ 1.414).

learn.reallife: Vacuum chambers at ISRO's test facilities pump air down so far that the mean free path becomes metres long, mimicking space conditions for satellites.

topics.title: Periodic and oscillatory motion

learn.hook: Your heartbeat, a jhoola at a mela, the hands of a clock and atoms in a crystal: all repeat their motion again and again.
points: Periodic and oscillatory motions are everywhere: swings, pendulums, heartbeats, vibrating strings and atoms in solids.
Oscillations underlie sound, waves of all kinds and alternating currents in electrical circuits.
Periodic motion repeats itself at regular intervals of time (the Earth's rotation, a clock's hands).

Oscillatory (vibratory) motion is to-and-fro motion about a mean (equilibrium) position. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory (uniform circular motion is periodic, not to-and-fro).
Oscillations happen because a restoring force acts towards the equilibrium position whenever the body is displaced.

example.q: Classify (a) the Moon going round the Earth and (b) a swinging jhoola.
steps: (a) The Moon repeats its path every 27.3 days, but does not move to and fro about a mean position: periodic, not oscillatory.
(b) The jhoola moves to and fro about its lowest point at regular intervals: oscillatory (and hence periodic).

learn.reallife: The quartz crystal in a digital watch oscillates 32768 times a second, keeping time for millions of Indians' wrists.

topics.title: Period, frequency and periodic functions

learn.hook: Indian classical tabla rhythms, alternating current at 50 Hz and a pendulum clock all have one thing in common: a definite period.
points: Period T: the smallest time after which the motion repeats. Frequency ν = 1/T (unit hertz, Hz = s⁻¹).
The displacement variable need not be a position. It can be an angle (pendulum), pressure (sound), voltage or current (AC), or electric and magnetic fields (light).
Any periodic function can be built as a sum of sines and cosines of different periods (Fourier's idea).

Checking periodicity: sin ωt, cos ωt and sin ωt + cos ωt are periodic with T = 2π/ω; sin²ωt is periodic with T = π/ω; sin ωt + cos 2ωt is periodic with T = 2π/ω (but not SHM); e^(−ωt) and log(ωt) are not periodic.

example.q: Find the period of x(t) = sin ωt + sin 2ωt.
steps: sin ωt has period 2π/ω; sin 2ωt has period π/ω.
The sum repeats only when both repeat.

learn.reallife: India's electricity grid runs at 50 Hz, so voltage in your home's sockets repeats every 0.02 s.

topics.title: Simple harmonic motion: displacement, amplitude and phase

learn.hook: A child on a spring rider at a park bounces up and down in a beautifully regular way. That motion is (nearly) simple harmonic.
points: SHM: displacement varies sinusoidally with time: x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ).
A = amplitude (maximum displacement, positive). (ωt + φ) = phase; φ = phase constant (epoch), the phase at t = 0. ω = angular frequency = 2π/T = 2πν.
On x–t graphs: a larger A gives taller curves; a different φ shifts the curve along the time axis; a larger ω squeezes it (shorter period).
To write the SHM equation, read A, T (hence ω) and the value of x at t = 0 (hence φ).

example.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and period 2 s, and starts at x = +5 cm at t = 0. Write x(t).
steps: A = 5 cm, ω = 2π/T = π rad s⁻¹.
At t = 0, x = A, so cos φ = 1 → φ = 0.

learn.reallife: Seismographs at IMD stations record ground vibrations as sinusoids; their amplitude and period reveal an earthquake's strength and distance.

topics.title: SHM as the projection of uniform circular motion

learn.hook: Shine a torch on a bead going round a turntable and watch its shadow on the wall: the shadow moves back and forth in perfect SHM.
points: If a particle moves uniformly on a circle, its projection (foot of the perpendicular) on any diameter executes SHM.
Reference circle: radius of the circle = amplitude A; angular speed of the particle = angular frequency ω of the SHM; initial angle = phase constant φ.
If the particle starts at angle φ from the x-axis and moves anticlockwise, its x-projection is x = A cos(ωt + φ) and its y-projection is y = A sin(ωt + φ).
Uniform circular motion = two perpendicular SHMs of equal amplitude with a phase difference of π/2.

example.q: A particle moves anticlockwise on a circle of radius 3 cm at 2 rev s⁻¹, starting at 60° from the +x axis. Write the SHM of its x-projection.
steps: A = 3 cm; ω = 2π × 2 = 4π rad s⁻¹; φ = π/3.

learn.reallife: Try it at home: put a cup near the edge of a slowly turning lazy-susan tray and shine a torch across the tray, level with it. The cup's shadow on the wall slides to and fro in SHM.

topics.title: Velocity and acceleration in SHM

learn.hook: A pendulum bob is fastest as it swings through the bottom and momentarily stops at the ends, where its acceleration is greatest.
points: Velocity: v = dx/dt = −ωA sin(ωt + φ). Maximum speed ωA at the mean position; zero at the extremes.
Speed in terms of displacement: v = ω√(A² − x²).
Acceleration: a = −ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x. It always points towards the mean position; maximum magnitude ω²A at the extremes, zero at the mean position.
Phase relations: velocity leads displacement by π/2; acceleration leads displacement by π (opposite to x).
Typical problems: find v_max = ωA and a_max = ω²A.

example.q: A body in SHM has A = 0.1 m and ω = 5 rad s⁻¹. Find its maximum speed, maximum acceleration, and speed at x = 0.06 m.

learn.reallife: Earthquake engineers at IIT Roorkee design buildings for the maximum ground acceleration ω²A, not just the displacement.

topics.title: The force law: springs and SHM

learn.hook: Stiffer shock absorbers on a mountain bike bounce faster. The period of a spring–mass system depends on the ratio m/k.
points: Force law for SHM: F = ma = −mω²x = −kx, with k = mω². The restoring force is linear in displacement and opposite to it.
So ω = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k).
A block of mass m on a spring of constant k on a frictionless surface is a linear harmonic oscillator.
Two identical springs (each k) attached to a block on opposite sides: displacing the block by x stretches one and compresses the other, so F = −2kx, k_eff = 2k and T = 2π√(m/2k).
Typical problem: given k and m, find T, then a_max = (k/m)A and v_max = A√(k/m).

example.q: A 1 kg block on a spring of k = 100 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Find T, v_max and a_max (π = 3.14).
example.answer: T ≈ 0.63 s; 1 m s⁻¹; 10 m s⁻²

learn.reallife: The suspension springs of an auto-rickshaw are chosen so that the bounce period is comfortable for passengers on bumpy roads.

topics.title: Energy in simple harmonic motion

learn.hook: A swing at the top of its arc is all potential energy; at the bottom it's all kinetic. The total never changes (if there's no friction).
points: Kinetic energy K = ½mv² = ½kA² sin²(ωt + φ). Potential energy U = ½kx² = ½kA² cos²(ωt + φ).
Total energy E = K + U = ½kA², constant. Energy keeps changing between kinetic and potential forms.
K and U each oscillate in time with period T/2 (twice per cycle), between 0 and ½kA².
Against displacement: U(x) = ½kx² is a parabola, K(x) = ½k(A² − x²) an inverted parabola; E is a horizontal line. K = U at x = ±A/√2.

example.q: A block (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with A = 0.1 m. Find E, and K and U at x = 0.05 m.

learn.reallife: Grandfather clocks in old Kolkata homes need winding because friction slowly drains the pendulum's total energy.

teach.praise: At the ends it's all PE, in the middle all KE, and the total ½kA² stays the same!
teach.nudge: What is the total energy in SHM? Where is it all kinetic, and where all potential?

topics.title: The simple pendulum

learn.hook: Galileo timed a swinging chandelier with his pulse and noticed something surprising: big or small swings, the time was the same.
points: A simple pendulum is a point mass (bob) hung from a light, inextensible string fixed at one end.
When displaced by θ, gravity gives a restoring torque τ = −mgL sin θ about the support.
For small angles, sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), so τ = −mgLθ: angular acceleration ∝ −θ, which is SHM.
Period T = 2π√(L/g). It is independent of the mass of the bob and (for small oscillations) of the amplitude.

example.q: Find the period of a pendulum of length 0.4 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻², π = 3.14).

learn.reallife: Pendulum clocks once kept time in Indian railway stations; adjusting the bob's height (L) corrected the clock.

topics.title: Seconds pendulum, measuring g and other SHMs

learn.hook: The 'seconds pendulum' takes exactly one second for each swing from one side to the other. Its length on Earth works out to very nearly 1 metre.
points: A seconds pendulum has a period of 2 s (each swing, one side to the other, takes 1 s). Its length L = gT²/(4π²) ≈ 0.99 m ≈ 1 m.
Measuring g: time many oscillations to find T, then g = 4π²L/T². Plotting T² against L gives a straight line of slope 4π²/g.
In a lift accelerating upward at a, the effective g is (g + a), so T decreases; accelerating downward, (g − a), T increases; in free fall, the pendulum does not oscillate.
On the Moon (g_Moon ≈ g/6), T is √6 times longer.

Other SHMs: a ball rolling in a smooth bowl near the bottom, liquid oscillating in a U-tube, a mass on springs. The Earth's rotation is periodic but not SHM; a polyatomic molecule's general vibration is a superposition of SHMs.

example.q: Find the length of a seconds pendulum where g = 9.8 m s⁻² (π² ≈ 9.87).

learn.reallife: Students in CBSE physics labs across India find g by timing 20 oscillations of a pendulum of known length; the class average is usually close to 9.8 m s⁻². Lab safety: clamp the stand firmly so it can't tip, and keep the swing small and clear of faces.

topics.title: What a wave is

learn.hook: A 'Mexican wave' sweeps around a packed Wankhede Stadium, yet no spectator leaves their seat. That's exactly how a wave works.
points: A wave transfers energy and information from one place to another without transporting matter as a whole.

Mechanical waves (sound, waves on strings, water waves, seismic waves) need a material medium. Electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays) do not need a medium. Matter waves are associated with moving particles like electrons.
In a mechanical wave, each particle of the medium only oscillates about its mean position; it is the disturbance (pattern) that travels.
Wave propagation needs two properties of the medium: elasticity (restoring forces between neighbouring parts) and inertia (mass) of its parts.

example.q: A paper boat floats on a pond as ripples pass. Does it move along with the ripples?
steps: The ripples carry energy across the water.
Each water particle, and the boat on it, just moves up and down (and slightly to and fro) about its place.
So the boat bobs but is not carried along by the wave.
example.answer: No, it only bobs about its position

learn.reallife: Mobile phone signals, Doordarshan broadcasts and the light from the Sun are electromagnetic waves; they travel even through the vacuum of space.

topics.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves

learn.hook: During an earthquake, the first jolt (P-wave) squeezes and stretches the ground; the later, more destructive shaking (S-wave) moves it side to side.
points: Transverse waves: particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation (wave on a string, ripples on a stretched rope).
Longitudinal waves: particles oscillate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions (sound in air, P-waves).

Transverse mechanical waves need the medium to resist shear (shear modulus), so they travel in solids and along strings, but not through the bulk of liquids or gases. Longitudinal waves travel in solids, liquids and gases.
Water surface waves are a combination of both: water particles move in roughly circular paths.
Classify by asking: do particles move across (transverse) or along (longitudinal) the direction the wave travels?

example.q: Classify: (a) sound from a sitar in air (b) the vibration of the sitar string (c) ripples on a lake.
steps: (a) Air particles oscillate along the direction of travel: longitudinal.
(b) The string vibrates perpendicular to its length: transverse.
(c) Water particles move in circles: both transverse and longitudinal.

learn.reallife: Seismologists at NCS (National Center for Seismology) use the arrival gap between P-waves and S-waves to locate earthquake epicentres.

topics.title: Equation of a progressive wave

learn.hook: One compact equation, y = a sin(kx − ωt + φ), describes the wave on a sitar string at every point and every instant.
points: A sinusoidal wave travelling in +x: y(x, t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ). In −x: y = a sin(kx + ωt + φ).
a = amplitude (maximum displacement). (kx − ωt + φ) = phase; φ = phase constant (initial phase at x = 0, t = 0).
Wavelength λ: distance between two consecutive points in the same phase (e.g. crests). Angular wave number k = 2π/λ (unit rad m⁻¹).
Period T: time for one oscillation of a particle; angular frequency ω = 2π/T; frequency ν = 1/T = ω/2π.
Reading a wave equation: match it with a sin(kx − ωt + φ) and identify a, k, ω, then λ = 2π/k, T = 2π/ω.

example.q: y = 0.005 sin(80x − 3t) (SI units). Find amplitude, wavelength, period and frequency.

learn.reallife: Engineers at All India Radio describe carrier waves by equations of exactly this form, with frequencies of hundreds of kHz.

topics.title: Wave speed and waves on strings

learn.hook: Tighten a sitar string and the note rises. Higher tension makes waves travel faster along the string.
points: Following a point of constant phase (kx − ωt = constant) gives the wave speed v = ω/k = λ/T = νλ.
Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium (elasticity and inertia), not on the frequency of the source. Changing the source frequency changes λ, not v.
Transverse wave on a stretched string: v = √(T/μ), where T is the tension and μ the mass per unit length. Dimensional analysis gives this form (constant = 1 from full theory).
Example: a wire of μ = 0.01 kg m⁻¹ under 100 N tension carries waves at √(100/0.01) = 100 m s⁻¹.

example.q: A 2 m wire of mass 0.04 kg is stretched with a tension of 50 N. Find the speed of a transverse pulse and the time to cross the wire.

learn.reallife: Sitar and veena players tune strings by adjusting tension with the pegs: v = √(T/μ) sets the pitch.

games.title: Finding the speed of a pulse on a wire
items: Find μ = mass/length
Note the tension T
Use v = √(T/μ)
For time to cross, divide length by v

Reason (R): Wave speed on a stretched string does not depend on its tension.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true (larger μ). R is false: v = √(T/μ) depends on tension.

teach.ask: Gappu tightens a vine and the twang sounds higher. Explain wave speed, v = νλ, and the speed on a stretched string.
teach.praise: Tighter vine, faster waves: v = √(T/μ). And speed is set by the medium, not the source!
teach.nudge: What two properties of a string set the wave speed? Does changing frequency change the speed?

topics.title: Speed of sound: Newton's formula and Laplace's correction

learn.hook: Put your ear to a railway track and you hear the train long before the sound comes through the air. Sound is much faster in steel.
points: Speed of longitudinal waves: v = √(B/ρ) in a fluid (B = bulk modulus), v = √(Y/ρ) in a solid rod.
Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases (e.g. roughly 5000 m s⁻¹ in steel, 1500 m s⁻¹ in water, 340 m s⁻¹ in air).
Newton assumed isothermal compressions: B = P, giving v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m s⁻¹ for air at STP, about 15% too low.
Laplace correction: compressions are fast and adiabatic, so B = γP and v = √(γP/ρ). With γ = 1.4 for air, v ≈ 331 m s⁻¹ at 0 °C, matching experiment.
v ∝ √T (absolute temperature). At constant temperature, changing pressure does not change v (since P/ρ stays constant).

example.q: Using Newton's formula, the speed of sound in air at STP comes out as 280 m s⁻¹. What does Laplace's correction give (γ = 1.4, √1.4 ≈ 1.183)?

learn.reallife: In a Rajasthan summer at 47 °C, sound travels noticeably faster than on a cold Shimla winter morning, because v ∝ √T.

Laplace: adiabatic, B = γP

Assertion (A): The speed of sound in air increases when the air pressure is increased at constant temperature.

quiz.explain: A is false: P/ρ is unchanged at constant temperature, so v is unchanged. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'Newton must have been right about the speed of sound.' Explain Newton's formula, Laplace's correction and how temperature and pressure affect v.
teach.praise: Newton used isothermal and got 280 m/s; Laplace used adiabatic (γP) and got 331 m/s! And v ∝ √T.
teach.nudge: What assumption did Newton make? How did Laplace fix it? What changes v: temperature or pressure?

topics.title: Using sound speed, and the superposition principle

learn.hook: During a monsoon storm, count the seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder, multiply by 340, and you know how far the strike was.
points: Echo: sound travels to the reflector and back, so distance d = vt/2.
Lightning–thunder: light arrives almost instantly, so distance ≈ v_sound × delay.
Principle of superposition: when two or more waves overlap, the net displacement at a point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements: y = y₁ + y₂ + ….
Two pulses moving in opposite directions pass through each other and emerge unchanged; while overlapping, they add (a crest and an equal trough momentarily cancel).

example.q: A girl shouts in front of a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s (v = 340 m s⁻¹). How far is the cliff?
steps: Sound goes to the cliff and back: total path = vt = 340 × 2 = 680 m.

learn.reallife: Bats over the forests of the Western Ghats use echoes to locate insects, timing returns to fractions of a millisecond.

items.q: Echo after 1 s: distance to wall (m)
y₁ = 3 mm, y₂ = −1 mm: net y (mm)

quiz.explain: Equal and opposite displacements cancel; the energy is then in the string's motion.

quiz.explain: Superposition is linear; each pulse moves on as before.

Assertion (A): The distance to a cliff is half the product of the speed of sound and the echo time.
Reason (R): The sound travels to the cliff and back, covering twice the distance.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Total path = 2d = vt, so d = vt/2. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu counted 3 seconds between a lightning flash and thunder. Teach him to find the distance, then explain superposition of waves.
teach.praise: About 1 km away! Echoes need a ÷2, and overlapping waves just add their displacements.
teach.nudge: How do you find the distance from the thunder delay? What happens when two waves overlap?

topics.title: Interference of two harmonic waves

learn.hook: Noise-cancelling headphones play a sound wave exactly opposite to the outside noise. The two add up to near silence.
points: Two waves of the same frequency and amplitude a, travelling in the same direction with phase difference φ: y₁ = a sin(kx − ωt), y₂ = a sin(kx − ωt + φ).
Resultant: y = 2a cos(φ/2) sin(kx − ωt + φ/2). The resultant amplitude is A = 2a cos(φ/2).
Constructive interference: φ = 0 (or 2nπ), A = 2a (intensity 4 times one wave).
Destructive interference: φ = π (or (2n + 1)π), A = 0.
Intermediate phases give amplitudes between 0 and 2a (e.g. φ = 2π/3 gives A = a).

example.q: Two waves of amplitude 3 mm and the same frequency travel together with a phase difference of π/2. Find the resultant amplitude.

learn.reallife: Concert halls like NCPA Mumbai are designed to avoid dead spots where reflected sound waves interfere destructively.

quiz.mistake: Thinks they add regardless of phase

quiz.explain: From adding the two sines.

quiz.mistake: Mixes up odd and even multiples

Assertion (A): Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency can cancel each other completely.
Reason (R): Two waves of equal amplitude always have equal frequencies.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true (phase difference π). R is false: amplitude and frequency are independent.

teach.ask: Gappu and a friend chirp the same note; sometimes it gets louder, sometimes nearly silent. Explain interference.
teach.praise: In phase, the amplitude doubles; out of phase by π, they cancel. A = 2a cos(φ/2) covers everything in between!
teach.nudge: What decides whether two waves reinforce or cancel? What is the resultant amplitude formula?

topics.title: Reflection and standing waves

learn.hook: Shake a rope tied to a wall at just the right rate and it forms a still pattern of loops. Waves going and coming back create a standing wave.
points: Reflection at a rigid boundary (fixed end): the reflected wave has a phase change of π, so a crest returns as a trough (pulse inverted).
Reflection at an open (free) boundary: no phase change; a crest returns as a crest.
The incident and reflected waves superpose to form a standing (stationary) wave: y = 2a sin kx cos ωt.
Nodes: points of zero amplitude (sin kx = 0): x = nλ/2. Antinodes: points of maximum amplitude 2a: x = (n + ½)λ/2.
Distance between adjacent nodes (or adjacent antinodes) = λ/2; between a node and the next antinode = λ/4.

example.q: A standing wave on a string has adjacent nodes 20 cm apart. Find the wavelength and the distance between a node and the nearest antinode.
steps: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart: λ = 40 cm.
Node to next antinode = λ/4 = 10 cm.

learn.reallife: Tabla and mridangam skins vibrate in standing-wave patterns; the black syahi patch shapes these modes to give their rich tones.

They are λ/2 apart.
A standing wave is formed by superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions.
Incident + reflected.

quiz.explain: The fixed end forces zero displacement, inverting the pulse.

Assertion (A): No energy is transported across a node in a standing wave.
Reason (R): Particles at a node never move, so no work is done across that point.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Zero displacement means no energy flow through a node. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks standing waves carry energy like travelling waves

teach.ask: Gappu ties a vine to a tree, shakes it and sees still loops. Explain reflection at boundaries and the formation of standing waves.
teach.praise: The reflected wave meets the incoming one, making nodes (no motion) and antinodes (big motion), λ/2 apart!
teach.nudge: What happens to a wave reflected from a fixed end? How far apart are neighbouring nodes?

topics.title: Normal modes of strings and air columns

learn.hook: A flute and a clarinet can play the same note, but they sound different. One is open at both ends, the other closed at one: different harmonics.
points: String fixed at both ends (nodes at both ends): λₙ = 2L/n, νₙ = nv/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … The lowest (n = 1) is the fundamental; all harmonics are present.
Air column closed at one end (node at closed end, antinode at open end): L = (2n − 1)λ/4, νₙ = (2n − 1)v/(4L). Only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) are present.
Air column open at both ends (antinodes at both ends): νₙ = nv/(2L); all harmonics are present.
For the same length, the fundamental of a closed pipe (v/4L) is half that of an open pipe (v/2L).

example.q: A string 0.5 m long carries waves at 200 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and the next two harmonics.

learn.reallife: The bansuri (bamboo flute) behaves like a pipe open at both ends; covering holes changes its effective length and so its notes.

teach.ask: Gappu blows across a bottle and then into a hollow reed open at both ends. Explain the normal modes of strings and pipes.
teach.praise: Strings and open pipes have all harmonics (nv/2L); closed pipes only odd ones ((2n − 1)v/4L)!
teach.nudge: Where are the nodes and antinodes in a closed pipe? Which harmonics does it allow?

topics.title: Resonance tube and harmonic numericals

learn.hook: In the CBSE physics lab, you lower a glass tube in water while a tuning fork hums above it. Suddenly it booms: resonance!
points: Resonance tube: an air column closed at the bottom by water. With a fork of frequency ν, resonance occurs when L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, …
Successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2: L₂ − L₁ = λ/2, so v = 2ν(L₂ − L₁). This removes the error of the end correction.
Harmonic numericals: for strings ν = nv/(2L) with v = √(T/μ); for closed pipes ν = (2n − 1)v/(4L); for open pipes ν = nv/(2L).
Check which harmonics are allowed before answering (e.g. a closed pipe can't give 2ν₁).

example.q: With a 500 Hz fork, resonances occur at 16.5 cm and 50.5 cm. Find the speed of sound.
steps: L₂ − L₁ = 34 cm = λ/2, so λ = 68 cm = 0.68 m.

learn.reallife: Resonance-tube experiments in Indian school labs routinely give the speed of sound within a few percent of 340 m s⁻¹. Lab safety: strike the tuning fork only on a rubber pad (never on the glass tube or the bench), and handle the glass tube gently to avoid breakage.

teach.ask: Gappu did the resonance-tube experiment and got two loud lengths. Teach him to find the speed of sound and to solve harmonic problems.
teach.praise: The gap between resonances is λ/2, so v = 2ν(L₂ − L₁). And closed pipes only allow odd harmonics!
teach.nudge: What does the difference between two resonance lengths equal? How do you get v from it?

topics.title: Beats

learn.hook: When two harmonium reeds are slightly out of tune, you hear a 'wah-wah-wah' throbbing. Those are beats.
points: Beats: periodic rise and fall (waxing and waning) of loudness heard when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies superpose.
Beat frequency = number of beats per second = |ν₁ − ν₂|.
Musicians tune instruments by sounding a note with a standard and adjusting until the beats disappear.

Unknown fork: if fork B gives n beats with a known fork A (ν_A), then ν_B = ν_A ± n. Loading B with wax lowers ν_B; filing its prongs raises ν_B. Watch whether beats increase or decrease to choose the sign.
Mixed numericals: read wave equations, standing waves on strings, organ pipes and beats.

example.q: A 512 Hz fork A gives 5 beats s⁻¹ with fork B. When B is loaded with a little wax, the beats fall to 3 s⁻¹. Find ν_B.
steps: Wax lowers ν_B. If ν_B = 517, it moves towards 512 and beats decrease ✓. If 507, beats would increase ✗.

learn.reallife: Sitar players tuning to a tanpura listen for beats; when the throbbing stops, the strings are in unison.

quiz.explain: The slow drifting phase difference makes loudness rise and fall.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

teach.ask: Gappu hears a 'wah-wah' when he and his sister hum nearly the same note. Explain beats and how to use them to find an unknown frequency.
teach.praise: The throb rate is the difference of frequencies! Tune until the beats vanish, and use wax or filing to solve fork puzzles.
teach.nudge: What causes beats? How is the beat frequency related to the two frequencies?
